concepts.title: A process is one program instance
concepts.text: PID identifies a process; PPID is its parent; USER is its owner. Several instances can share a command name. Use ps and pgrep -u OWNER -x NAME to identify the intended supplied instance.

concepts.title: Read its current state
concepts.text: In STAT, R means running, S waiting and T paused. NI is a nice value, a scheduling preference taught later. Inspect the actual process after sending a request; a successful request can print nothing.

concepts.title: Pause without ending
concepts.text: kill sends a signal. STOP pauses a process but keeps it present; CONT resumes it. Do not send TERM for a pause task: while paused, an ending request can wait to be delivered when it continues.

concepts.title: An ending request can wait
concepts.text: TERM asks a process to end. A paused worker in this model retains that request until it can run again; sending TERM repeatedly does not continue it.

concepts.title: Two supported ways to finish
concepts.text: CONT lets the paused worker run and receive the pending TERM. KILL ends the modeled worker immediately, even while paused. Real programs may handle TERM differently; this fixed model excludes custom handlers and uninterruptible waits.

concepts.title: Verify absence

goal: Distinguish a shared file from a copy by inspecting identity and future edits.
context: Builds on files, paths and safe file handovers. Each introduction teaches the new link behavior before practice.

concepts.title: A name is not the stored file
concepts.text: A directory maps each name to an inode: the stored file and its data. A hard link adds another name for the same regular file. ln SOURCE NEW_NAME creates that name; removing one name does not remove the remaining aliases.

concepts.title: A copy becomes independent
concepts.text: cp SOURCE NEW_NAME creates an independent inode with initially equal data. ls -i DIRECTORY pairs each visible name with its own inode number: hard-link names match, while an independent copy differs. Equal text alone proves neither relationship; stat also shows type and link count.

concepts.title: Test what happens after an edit
concepts.text: The terminal operates on simulated files. In the optional file editor, open an existing file, edit its text and Save file. Then cat each name to compare shared changes with a retained snapshot.

requirements: Use /delivery/live as a hard-link name for /work/report.
Create an independent copy at /archive/snapshot.
Retain Release notes v1 plus a newline in both files and preserve /work/keep.
Future edits through either live name must affect both; the snapshot must remain independent.

worked.label: Example action 1
worked.explanation: Adds another name for the same regular inode; stat through both names should report the same identity.

worked.label: Example action 2
worked.explanation: Creates a separate regular inode with equal starting text. Later changes to the source must leave this copy unchanged.

worked.label: Example action 3
worked.explanation: Type and Run ls -i /practice/in for a names-and-inodes view, then use this stat command to inspect the file type and link count as well.

worked.label: Example action 4
worked.explanation: Compare the actual inode, type and link count. -L follows a final symbolic link instead of inspecting the link itself.

worked.label: Example action 5
worked.explanation: Compare the actual inode, type and link count. -L follows a final symbolic link instead of inspecting the link itself.

practice.title: Create two different relationships
practice.action: Insert and Run ln /practice/in/brief /practice/out/live, then cp /practice/in/brief /practice/archive/copy.
practice.observe: ln adds a name for the same inode; cp creates an independent file.

practice.title: Compare names before editing

practice.observe: brief and live share one virtual inode. copy has another, even though its starting text matches. The numbers identify this simulation only.

practice.observe: Both hard-link names show the edit; the copied file keeps its previous text.

goal: Make a symbolic link resolve from its containing directory.
context: Builds on files, paths and safe file handovers. Each introduction teaches the new link behavior before practice.

concepts.title: A symbolic link stores a path
concepts.text: ln -s TARGET NEW_LINK stores text naming a target. It has its own inode and can exist while its target is missing. readlink LINK shows that stored text; cat LINK follows it.

concepts.title: Start relative targets beside the link
concepts.text: For /practice/out/latest, ../in/today starts in /practice/out and reaches /practice/in/today. Your terminal’s /work directory is irrelevant to that calculation. An absolute target starts at the simulated root.

concepts.title: Inspect the link and the destination separately
concepts.text: ls -i DIRECTORY shows each visible name’s own inode, so a symbolic link has an identity separate from its target. It does not show the target text: readlink does that. stat LINK inspects the link, while stat -L LINK follows it. Removing the link leaves the target intact.

requirements: Repair /delivery/latest as a symbolic link to /work/current.
Relative and absolute targets are accepted when they resolve correctly.
Preserve the original current file, its identity and /work/keep.

worked.label: Example action 1
worked.explanation: Type and Run ls -i /practice/out to see the shortcut’s own identity. This readlink command then shows its stored target text, even while following it fails.

worked.label: Example action 2
worked.explanation: Removes this one name. A symbolic target or another hard-link name stays intact.

worked.label: Example action 3
worked.explanation: Stores the target path in a new symbolic link. Relative targets start in the link’s containing directory.

worked.label: Example action 4
worked.explanation: Compare the actual inode, type and link count. -L follows a final symbolic link instead of inspecting the link itself.

worked.label: Example action 5
worked.explanation: Follows the path and shows its actual file contents; a dangling target produces an error.

practice.title: Inspect the shortcut itself
practice.action: Type and Run ls -i /practice/out, then Insert readlink /practice/out/latest and Run. Use cat /practice/out/latest to test the target.
practice.observe: The link has its own inode even when dangling. readlink shows stored text; neither an inode number nor the name alone proves that following it succeeds.

practice.title: Repair and follow it
practice.action: Run rm /practice/out/latest, then ln -s ../in/today /practice/out/latest. Insert stat -L and Run, then Check example.
practice.observe: The .. moves from /practice/out to /practice before in/today is followed.

practice.title: Try a change and explain it
practice.action: After practice passes, remove latest and recreate it with target in/today; run cat through it. Then restore ../in/today.
practice.observe: The broken target starts at /practice/out, not at /practice. readlink succeeds while following it fails.

goal: Preserve a moved file and repair the name pointing to its former location.
context: Builds on files, paths and safe file handovers. Each introduction teaches the new link behavior before practice.

concepts.title: Moving a name retains its inode
concepts.text: mv SOURCE NEW_NAME moves a name while keeping its inode in this single-device subset. Record it with stat or ls -i DIRECTORY before moving, then compare the destination’s inode. Copy followed by removal makes a different inode; existing destinations are unsupported.

concepts.title: Stored link text does not follow a rename
concepts.text: A symbolic link still stores its old target text after the file is moved. readlink can succeed while cat fails because that target no longer exists. Inspect the intended destination before repairing the link.

concepts.title: Repair the shortcut, preserve the file
concepts.text: Remove and recreate the symbolic link so it reaches the new file location. Compare stat identity and cat contents, then check the complete handover rather than only the shortcut.

worked.label: Example action 3

practice.observe: Moving the original receipt back leaves the link pointing at its now-missing archive path. Moving it to the archive again restores access without changing its inode or rewriting the link.

goal: Combine hard links, independent copies and a symbolic publication link safely.
context: Builds on files, paths and safe file handovers. Each introduction teaches the new link behavior before practice.

concepts.title: Use each link type for its job
concepts.text: Keep the old file available through a hard-link name; preserve an independent copy as a snapshot. A symbolic link is a convenient publication name for the new version.

concepts.title: Retiring a name is not deleting every alias
concepts.text: After creating the retained hard link, rm the old name. The retained name still refers to the original inode. A copy may have the right contents while failing the identity requirement.

concepts.title: Verify the whole change
concepts.text: Use ls -i DIRECTORY to compare the pin and snapshot identities, then inspect the publication link with readlink or stat -L. Keep old data and the new target intact. The grader also tries future edits to detect a shared alias pretending to be an independent snapshot.

worked.explanation: Removes this one name. A symbolic target or another hard-link name stays intact.

goal: Separate an enabled source, its cached index and package query results.
requirements: Enable tools using the supplied updates source and cache its current published metadata.
Query exact package for parcel and companion. Both must show only the tools candidate from the current snapshot.
Inspect candidates only; this task does not install or download packages.
context: Builds on RPM package records. Here configuration, metadata and query evidence are simulated; no software is installed and no source address is opened.

concepts.title: A repository is a package source
concepts.text: Repository metadata is an index describing available packages. Configuration says where a source is and whether it participates; a cache holds metadata already copied from it. Neither is an installed program.

concepts.title: Enabled does not mean refreshed
concepts.text: Enabling a source makes it eligible for queries. A source with no cached metadata still has no candidates. Refresh metadata copies its supplied published index in this simulation; it does not install software.

concepts.title: Query the index you actually have
concepts.text: Query exact package reads cached metadata without silently refreshing it. An empty result can mean a disabled source or missing cache, not just an unknown package. Read the omission message.

practice.title: Diagnose the empty sample
practice.action: Enter sample-parcel and choose Query exact package before changing anything. Read the omission.
practice.observe: practice is disabled; an explicit Refresh metadata also refuses until it is enabled.

practice.title: Enable, refresh, inspect
practice.action: Choose practice, select Enabled for queries, then Apply settings. Choose Refresh metadata. Query sample-parcel, then sample-companion, and Check example.
practice.observe: Both actual queries now read the new cached snapshot. No package has been installed.

practice.title: Distinguish a filter from data loss
practice.action: Disable practice and Apply settings; query again. Read the disabled omission. Enable it again, Apply, and query both names before Check example.
practice.observe: The cache remains present while disabled. Applied setting changes make earlier inspection evidence stale.

worked.label: Enable the sample
worked.explanation: Apply settings changes only configuration.

worked.label: Refresh its index
worked.explanation: The available supplied source provides metadata, not an installed program.

worked.label: Inspect both names
worked.explanation: The actual table shows source, snapshot and version for each query.

review.introduction: Teaches repository configuration versus metadata cache versus installed software, then demonstrates separate sample source enabling, refresh and two exact-name queries.
review.example: Actual native practice reveals disabled and missing-cache omissions, applies configuration and metadata separately, then diagnoses a disabled source without losing its cache.

goal: Distinguish cache age from which source produced the cache.
requirements: Make tools use the supplied updates source, enabled for queries, with matching current metadata.
Query parcel and companion; retain only the tools candidates from the current updates snapshot.
A matching current cache can be reused. Refresh explicitly only when the applied source and cached metadata require it.
context: Builds on RPM package records. Here configuration, metadata and query evidence are simulated; no software is installed and no source address is opened.

concepts.title: A cache belongs to a source
concepts.text: A snapshot name is not enough to identify where metadata came from. Compare the configured source with the cached endpoint. This model withholds candidate rows when those identities disagree.

concepts.title: Changing an address does not rewrite history
concepts.text: Apply settings changes the configured URI, but retains the old cached endpoint and snapshot. If the old cache already belongs to the newly selected source and is current, it can be reused. Otherwise refresh from the intended available source.

concepts.title: Investigate before refreshing
concepts.text: A refresh replaces cached metadata with that source’s published snapshot. Refreshing a mistaken address can replace useful evidence with the wrong index. First identify the intended source and inspect the retained cache.

practice.title: Find the mismatch
practice.action: Query sample-parcel. Compare practice’s configured source with its cached source in the inspection table.
practice.observe: The cache came from sample-updates, while the current address names sample-archive. Different source is not simply Older snapshot.

practice.title: Repair configuration, then query
practice.action: Set practice’s URI to the supplied sample-updates address and Apply settings. Query sample-parcel and sample-companion; Check example.
practice.observe: The retained cache already matches this source’s current publication, so a refresh is unnecessary. An explicit refresh followed by both queries also works.

practice.title: Observe a wrong refresh
practice.action: Change practice to sample-archive, Apply settings and Refresh metadata, then query. Restore sample-updates, Apply and Refresh, query both names and check again.
practice.observe: The old archive snapshot replaces the cache. Merely changing back leaves wrong-source metadata until you refresh updates.

worked.label: Configured sample source
worked.explanation: Its URI does not match the cache’s provenance.

worked.label: Cached sample source
worked.explanation: This is useful metadata for the intended source.

worked.label: Repair and inspect
worked.explanation: A matching current cache is reusable; no ritual refresh is required.

review.introduction: Separates source provenance from snapshot age and explains why a useful matching current cache can be reused without a ritual refresh.
review.example: Separate source mismatch is repaired through the native editor; the deliberate wrong refresh shows changed provenance and requires repair plus new evidence.
review.assignment: Independent intended-source/current-cache requirement and two actual queries, accepting both cache reuse and explicit refresh alternatives; no canned row grading.

goal: Preserve useful offline evidence without calling it current metadata.
requirements: Retain tools configuration and its existing cached source/snapshot exactly. The supplied updates delivery fact is Unavailable.
Query parcel and companion using the retained older cache. Both actual results must come only from tools.
Read the Older snapshot label and recorded version. This is cached evidence, not proof of current remote contents or a successful installation.
context: Builds on RPM package records. Here configuration, metadata and query evidence are simulated; no software is installed and no source address is opened.

concepts.title: Unavailable is not empty
concepts.text: Delivery availability and cached metadata are different facts. A matching older cache can still describe packages when the source cannot currently supply a refresh. Reading that index does not contact the real network.

concepts.title: State what the evidence supports
concepts.text: The table identifies the cached snapshot and package version. Older snapshot means it predates the supplied current publication. It does not prove the remote source still has the same packages or that an installation would succeed.

concepts.title: A failed refresh must not destroy evidence
concepts.text: Refresh metadata against the unavailable sample refuses without replacing its cache. Preserve the old index and query it explicitly. Do not change the address merely to hide an honest offline result.

practice.title: Inspect before repairing
practice.action: Read practice’s source availability, cached endpoint and Older snapshot label. Query sample-parcel and sample-companion, then Check example.
practice.observe: Both versions come from old cached metadata. No configuration repair is needed for this evidence task.

practice.title: Try an expected refusal
practice.action: Choose Refresh metadata for practice, then query a name again. Read the refusal and cache identity.
practice.observe: Unavailable delivery leaves the useful old cache unchanged; the query remains an offline metadata inspection.

practice.title: Compare a different source
practice.action: Change practice to sample-archive and Apply settings, then query. Restore its original sample-updates address, Apply, query both names and check.
practice.observe: The wrong-source query is withheld. Restoring the original matching source permits the old cache again; no false freshness is invented.

worked.label: Delivery fact
worked.explanation: This is a supplied simulator fact, not a live network probe.

worked.label: Retained cache
worked.explanation: Matching provenance makes the older index usable for inspection.

worked.label: Query outcome
worked.explanation: Report the actual cached versions without claiming they are current.

review.introduction: Teaches unavailable delivery versus a useful older matching cache, honest evidence limits and failed-refresh retention before the independent investigation.
review.example: Separate sample queries show actual old versions; unavailable refresh refuses atomically, while address changes demonstrate wrong-source withholding and recovery.
review.assignment: Independent preservation and multi-package evidence task, without forcing unnecessary configuration changes; actual older snapshot remains labeled and no false freshness is awarded.

goal: Repair one repository and preserve another repository’s configuration and cache.
requirements: Make live use the supplied updates source, enabled with matching current metadata.
Keep held disabled at its original address and preserve its original cached source/snapshot.
Query parcel and companion after the changes. Each must show only the current live candidate, with no held candidates.
Verify both repositories; a successful query for one package is only partial completion.
context: Builds on RPM package records. Here configuration, metadata and query evidence are simulated; no software is installed and no source address is opened.

concepts.title: Treat each repository separately
concepts.text: An alias names a configuration record. Two aliases can point at the same source but keep separate cached snapshots. Repairing live must not overwrite held’s historical state.

concepts.title: Check policy as well as a positive result
concepts.text: An unwanted enabled source can add older candidates to a query. A handover must verify the desired current source and the absence of held candidates, not just find one acceptable row.

concepts.title: Reinspect after the final edit
concepts.text: Queries describe the cache state at the time you ran them. Refreshes or applied configuration changes make earlier handover evidence stale; query both required packages after the final change.

practice.title: Compare both sample aliases
practice.action: Inspect practice-live and practice-held, then query sample-parcel.
practice.observe: Both caches are old, but practice-held is intentionally disabled and must stay unchanged.

practice.title: Repair only the live sample
practice.action: Point practice-live at sample-updates, Apply settings and Refresh metadata. Query sample-parcel and sample-companion; Check example.
practice.observe: The live cache becomes current. The held configuration and historical cache remain intact.

practice.title: Catch an extra candidate
practice.action: Enable practice-held and Apply settings, then query and check. Restore it to disabled, Apply, query both names and retry.
practice.observe: An old held candidate is still unwanted even when the current live candidate is present. Final evidence must follow the repair.

worked.label: Repair scope
worked.explanation: Use the supplied sample-updates source and refresh its index.

worked.label: Retained scope
worked.explanation: Keep its disabled state, address and cached archive snapshot.

worked.label: Evidence set
worked.value: Query both sample package names after all edits
worked.explanation: Positive rows and omitted held candidates matter together.

review.introduction: Explains independent alias/cache records, positive and excluded candidate policies, and rerunning evidence after the final applied change.
review.example: Native sample repairs only live, preserves held, then demonstrates an unwanted held candidate and retries with both required package queries.
review.assignment: Full independent two-repository handover with protected config/cache, current-source evidence and negative held-candidate checks; starter errors and hidden solution preserved.

review.introduction: Separately teaches administrative state, correct LAN address/prefix and the one-primary subset; demonstrates exact sample delete/add/up commands before the task.
review.example: Guides inspection, sample repair and deliberate link failure beside the terminal and simulator path test; example IPs/world/drafts are separate.
review.assignment: Requires an unused address, two LAN paths and preserved management; native terminal/check feedback allows alternate addresses, not exact command strings.

goal: Investigate link state and address/prefix separately, then verify the supplied LAN.
requirements: Bring ens3 up and configure one unused conventional host address in 192.0.2.0/24. Do not use network/broadcast or any supplied peer/gateway address.
Provide usable virtual LAN paths to 192.0.2.20 and 192.0.2.200 through ens3.
Keep ens4’s complete management interface state and the 10.40.0.0/24 route unchanged.
context: This unit uses supplied virtual host facts and a simulated administrator terminal. No sudo, host network or host files are used. Interface addresses use conventional /1–/30 LANs; route prefixes have different bounds.

concepts.title: A link and its address are different settings
concepts.text: An interface is the computer’s connection to a LAN. Administratively down means it has been switched off in configuration. An IPv4 address identifies the computer on that LAN; /24 describes which addresses it treats as nearby. Fixing one setting does not fix the other.

concepts.title: Inspect before changing
concepts.text: ip link show displays the modeled administrative/link state. ip -4 address show displays the configured IPv4 address and prefix. Compare both with the supplied LAN facts; an address from another LAN will not work just because the link is up.

concepts.title: Replace only the intended virtual address
concepts.text: This activity models one primary IPv4 address per interface. Delete the old address/prefix, add an unused address in the supplied LAN, then bring the interface up. Full Linux supports additional addresses; this subset reports that limit instead of pretending to replace them.

practice.title: Investigate the sample
practice.action: Run ip link show and ip -4 address show. Compare ens3 with the supplied sample LAN; leave ens4 alone.
practice.observe: ens3 is down and has an address from a different LAN. These are two separate faults.

practice.title: Repair the sample connection
practice.action: Delete 10.90.0.10/24 from ens3, add 10.71.0.10/24, then set ens3 up. Use Test address for 10.71.0.20 and 10.71.0.200, then Check example.
practice.observe: Both virtual LAN paths should work. A different unused /24 address in the same LAN also passes.

practice.title: Diagnose a deliberate mistake
practice.action: Set ens3 down and Check example. Read the link/path feedback, set it up again and retry.
practice.observe: An address can remain configured while the interface is down. Management state must remain unchanged.

worked.label: Inspect first
worked.explanation: Administrative state is separate from the IPv4 address.

worked.label: Remove sample error
worked.explanation: The exact supplied address/prefix is removed from the virtual interface.

worked.label: Add sample address
worked.explanation: This is one unused address on the sample LAN, not the graded LAN.

worked.label: Bring the link up
worked.value: ip link set dev ens3 up
worked.explanation: Inspect again, then use the simulator’s native Test address control.

review.introduction: Explains default routes, longest prefix before lower Linux metric, configured preference versus unavailable supplied gateways; uses a separate worked host.
review.example: Guides actual route inspection, both sample repairs and a deliberate high-metric /32 override; native path evidence identifies the affected target.
review.assignment: Requires three healthy paths and preferred default while retaining both interfaces/management route; valid removal, metric and replacement repairs pass.

goal: Use prefix length before metric, and verify actual supplied path availability.
requirements: Make the preferred configured default use 198.51.100.1 on ens4; the supplied ens3 gateway is unavailable.
Provide usable virtual paths to 203.0.113.53, 203.0.113.80 and 203.0.113.90 through ens4. Inspect more-specific routes as well as defaults.
Keep both interface configurations and every 10.40.0.0/24 management route entry unchanged.
context: This unit uses supplied virtual host facts and a simulated administrator terminal. No sudo, host network or host files are used. Interface addresses use conventional /1–/30 LANs; route prefixes have different bounds.

concepts.title: A route chooses where traffic should go
concepts.text: A gateway route names a destination prefix, a next hop and an outgoing interface. default covers addresses without a more-specific matching route. The supplied gateway facts say whether this virtual onward path is available; no real packets or timing are measured.

concepts.title: Longest prefix wins first
concepts.text: A /32 host route matches one destination more specifically than a /0 default. A high metric on that /32 does not make a default take precedence. First compare prefix lengths; only then compare metrics between equally specific routes.

concepts.title: Lower metric is not proof of a usable path
concepts.text: For matching routes of the same prefix length, the lower Linux metric is preferred in this model. A configured low-metric gateway can still be unavailable. Repair the route policy and test all required destinations, rather than assuming one successful path proves the whole table.

practice.title: Read the sample table
practice.action: Run ip -4 route show. Use Test address for the three sample remote destinations. Compare the selected prefixes with the supplied gateway availability.
practice.observe: The low-metric default is not usable. A separate /32 route also overrides a healthy default for one destination.

practice.title: Repair both sample decisions
practice.action: Remove the default via 10.71.0.1 with metric 10 and the 10.73.0.80/32 route via 10.71.0.1 with metric 999. Test the three addresses and Check example.
practice.observe: The remaining healthy default now serves all required targets. Raising metrics or replacing the host route can also be valid when every requirement passes.

practice.title: Try a more-specific override
practice.action: Add 10.73.0.80/32 via 10.71.0.1 dev ens3 metric 4000, then Check example. Remove that exact route and retry.
practice.observe: Even a very high metric cannot make a /32 lose to a default. The feedback identifies the affected virtual path.

worked.label: Compare defaults
worked.explanation: A lower configured metric wins, but the first supplied gateway is unavailable.

worked.label: Notice the host route
worked.explanation: Its longer prefix overrides both defaults for that one destination.

worked.label: Repair the sample
worked.value: Remove the unusable default and host route
worked.explanation: Verify all three supplied targets; preserve the separate management route.

review.introduction: Teaches IP-path versus name lookup, nameserver lines, ordered supplied resolvers and wrong records before editing; different worked resolver text shown.
review.example: Guides native path test, getent queries and virtual editor save, then compares a reachable wrong resolver; practice remains independent of assignment.
review.assignment: Requires two actual name outcomes and preserved healthy interfaces/default/management routes; unsaved virtual text cannot pass, no host DNS/file used.

goal: Repair the virtual client resolver without changing healthy interfaces or routes.
requirements: Resolve service.lab.test to 203.0.113.80 and inventory.lab.test to 203.0.113.90 using the supplied virtual resolver data.
Keep the already-working IP path to 203.0.113.80 and both interface configurations unchanged.
Preserve the default-route entries and 10.40.0.0/24 management routes. Edit only the virtual /etc/resolv.conf as needed.
Only IPv4 nameserver lines and comments are supported. Save the editor before checking; no host file is changed.
context: This unit uses supplied virtual host facts and a simulated administrator terminal. No sudo, host network or host files are used. Interface addresses use conventional /1–/30 LANs; route prefixes have different bounds.

concepts.title: A name lookup is not an IP-path test
concepts.text: A computer needs a usable network path and appropriate name-resolution settings. If Test address succeeds for the supplied service IP while a name lookup fails, changing healthy interface addresses is not the first repair.

concepts.title: A nameserver line selects a resolver
concepts.text: In this virtual /etc/resolv.conf, nameserver followed by an IPv4 address chooses a supplied resolver. Saving the native editor changes only this lesson’s resolver state. getent ahostsv4 NAME uses those supplied A records; it never asks the real network.

concepts.title: Order and answers both matter
concepts.text: The first reachable supplied resolver returns its answer, including a negative answer. The model tries the next server only when the earlier one is unavailable or unreachable. A reachable resolver with the wrong supplied record is different from a broken IP path.

practice.title: Compare IP and name evidence
practice.action: Use Test address for 10.73.0.80. Run getent ahostsv4 service.lab.test and inspect the virtual resolver editor.
practice.observe: The IP path is usable, but the configured address is not a supplied resolver for this task.

practice.title: Repair only the sample resolver
practice.action: Put nameserver 10.73.0.53 in the virtual editor and Save resolver. Run getent ahostsv4 service.lab.test and getent ahostsv4 inventory.lab.test, then Check example.
practice.observe: The two actual A answers now match the sample requirements. The healthy interface and route state remains unchanged.

practice.title: Compare another supplied answer
practice.action: Change the first nameserver to 10.73.0.54, Save and check. Read the actual wrong answers, restore 10.73.0.53 and retry.
practice.observe: A working path to a reachable resolver does not guarantee the record data meets the task. A second server is not automatically used after a negative answer.

worked.label: Isolate the fault
worked.explanation: This simulator operation checks supplied path facts, not DNS.

worked.label: Virtual resolver text
worked.explanation: Save resolver applies only this sample’s editable text.

worked.label: Read actual A records
worked.explanation: This reads supplied records through the configured virtual resolver, with no host lookup.

review.introduction: Builds on the three prior host activities; teaches dependency order and protected management, with a different complete sample handover.
review.example: Guides full host inspection, application repair and checks of both service and management; deliberate management/DNS damage provides meaningful retry.
review.assignment: Full terminal/resolver task requires alternate-valid address/default, application paths, two DNS answers and retained management; no solution exposed by default.

goal: Combine interface, route and resolver repair without disturbing the separate management path.
requirements: Repair ens3 with one unused conventional 192.0.2.0/24 address and bring it up. Make the preferred default use 192.0.2.1 on ens3.
Provide virtual application paths to 203.0.113.80 and 203.0.113.90 through ens3; resolve service.lab.test and inventory.lab.test to those respective addresses.
Retain ens4’s complete management state and every 10.40.0.0/24 route entry. The management path to 10.40.0.20 must still use ens4.
Save any virtual resolver changes before checking. Valid address/metric choices are accepted when all required outcomes hold.
context: This unit uses supplied virtual host facts and a simulated administrator terminal. No sudo, host network or host files are used. Interface addresses use conventional /1–/30 LANs; route prefixes have different bounds.

concepts.title: Plan both the repair and the protected path
concepts.text: The application and management interfaces serve different LANs. Before editing, identify the application address/default/resolver faults and the management state that must remain intact. A successful application lookup is not permission to disturb management.

concepts.title: Follow the dependencies
concepts.text: Bring up the intended application interface with a correct address, then configure a usable default through its on-link supplied gateway. Only then can a remote supplied resolver and service become reachable. A nameserver edit alone cannot repair a broken IP path.

concepts.title: Verify independent outcomes
concepts.text: Check application paths, both required name answers and the retained management route. State-based grading accepts safe alternative addresses, metrics and operation orders; it does not require reproducing one exact command sequence.

practice.title: Inspect the complete sample
practice.action: Run ip link show, ip -4 address show and ip -4 route show. Compare the supplied LAN/gateway facts and the resolver text.
practice.observe: The management interface is already correct. The application interface and default/resolver policy need repair.

practice.title: Perform a sample handover
practice.action: Repair ens3 on 10.71.0.0/24, bring it up, add a preferred default through 10.71.0.1, then save nameserver 10.73.0.53. Test both application IPs and 10.74.0.20, run both name lookups and Check example.
practice.observe: Application traffic uses ens3 while the more-specific management route still uses ens4. All checks matter together.

practice.title: Catch a partial repair
practice.action: Set ens4 down and check. Restore it, then try the alternate supplied resolver and read the resulting name failures. Restore the correct sample state and retry.
practice.observe: Working application traffic cannot compensate for lost management, and a reachable resolver can still provide the wrong answer.

worked.label: Application address
worked.explanation: Delete the wrong sample primary before adding this different address.

worked.label: Application default
worked.explanation: This lower-metric default does not replace the more-specific management route.

worked.label: Resolver
worked.explanation: Save the virtual text and inspect both supplied names.

worked.label: Protected management
worked.explanation: Test the management destination as well as the repaired application paths.

goal: Configure a severity threshold and check both included and excluded events.
requirements: Route every facility at warning(4) or more urgent levels0–3 exactly once to /var/log/operations.log.
Do not deliver notice, info or debug events, and do not use other destinations.

practice.title: Compare the starter with the policy
practice.action: The practice policy is mail at crit2 or more urgent, once to service.log. Compare the = in the editor with the threshold explanation.
practice.observe: A single correct mail.crit sample is insufficient; alert1 and emerg0 must reach the same destination.

practice.title: Run and inspect, then repair
practice.action: Select Run routing test on the starter. Read its required-versus-actual feedback, edit the selector or use Insert worked configuration, then run again.
practice.observe: The actual replay shows the supplied sample events. The outcome check also tests cases not present in that small sample.

practice.title: Try a broader threshold
practice.action: Change mail.crit to mail.err and run again, then restore the worked configuration.
practice.observe: The broader threshold adds mail.err events that this practice policy does not request.

review.introduction: Teaches facility, named severity order and inclusive urgency thresholds; worked mail.crit uses different data and demonstrates missing more-urgent messages.
review.example: Guides running the faulty exact-only sample, repairing its threshold and broadening it deliberately; actual sample includes mail emerg/alert/crit to make the difference visible.
review.assignment: Independent all-facility warning policy requires included and excluded severities with no extra destinations; full192-combination grading accepts alternate exact-level partitions.

worked.label: Worked configuration
worked.explanation: Different sample policy: Configure a severity threshold and check both included and excluded events.

concepts.title: Two labels on each log record
concepts.text: A log records something that happened. Its facility identifies the producing subsystem, such as mail or daemon. Its severity describes urgency: emerg0, alert1, crit2, err3, warning4, notice5, info6, debug7. A smaller number is more urgent.

concepts.title: Write a source and a threshold
concepts.text: A classic selector has facility.level followed by a destination path. In the worked example, mail.crit selects mail events at crit2 and also alert1 and emerg0. It does not select mail.err3, or another facility. * as the facility means every facility.

concepts.title: Test the boundaries, not just one event
concepts.text: The optional = means exactly one level. mail.=crit omits the more urgent mail events, so it cannot implement a crit-or-more-urgent policy. Run routing test checks included and excluded events; every destination here is a simulated file.

goal: Use an exact level without losing the broader urgent-event stream.
requirements: Route daemon events at exactly info(6) once to /var/log/service.log.
Independently route all facilities at err(3) or more urgent once to /var/log/operations.log.
Deliver no other copies or records.

practice.title: Read both practice streams
practice.action: The practice policy needs cron at exactly notice5 in service.log, and all facilities through crit2 in operations.log. Compare the two editor lines.
practice.observe: The first rule must be exact; the second must be a threshold.

practice.title: Test and repair the exact match
practice.action: Run routing test, inspect the extra cron deliveries, then edit only that selector or Insert worked configuration and run again.
practice.observe: Changing the exact-level stream must preserve urgent alerts.

practice.title: Observe overlapping rules
practice.action: Add cron.=notice /var/log/service.log as another line and run, then remove that extra line.
practice.observe: Two matching rules to the same destination deliver two copies; there is no automatic deduplication.

review.introduction: Teaches exact-level selection versus urgent thresholds in separate destination streams; worked cron notice and all-facility critical rules introduce the distinction.
review.example: Guides sample repair with visible cron notice and err events, then duplicate-rule exploration; worked fill changes only the separate draft and never executes automatically.
review.assignment: Requires the declared exact daemon stream and urgent general stream, retaining independent rules; feedback distinguishes extra lower-number levels and missing required copies.

worked.label: Worked configuration
worked.explanation: Different sample policy: Use an exact level without losing the broader urgent-event stream.

concepts.title: Routine reports can need exactly one level
concepts.text: An info or notice report is not always an urgency threshold. The worked policy needs cron events only at notice5, so cron.=notice selects that single level. Without =, it also includes more urgent cron events.

concepts.title: Lines are independent rules
concepts.text: The second worked line *.crit selects every facility at emerg0, alert1 or crit2. It does not stop processing the first line or redirect an earlier delivery. Each line that matches delivers another copy.

concepts.title: Keep the task as a routing policy
concepts.text: Read both destination requirements before editing. A selector that fixes one file can still add unwanted events elsewhere. The checks evaluate the whole configuration and detect duplicate copies.

goal: Exclude one source from a broad rule while retaining its private records.
requirements: Route all authpriv levels0–7 exactly once to /var/log/private.log.
Route all other facilities at info(6) or more urgent exactly once to /var/log/operations.log.
Keep authpriv out of operations.log, exclude other-facility debug, and leave service.log empty.

practice.title: Locate the privacy leak
practice.action: The practice policy keeps all authpriv levels in private.log and all other sources through notice5 in operations.log. Inspect both starter lines.
practice.observe: A matching private rule does not prevent a general-log copy.

practice.title: Repair and rerun
practice.action: Run routing test to see leaked and missing records. Edit the exclusions and private selection, or Insert worked configuration, then run.
practice.observe: The private alert must appear only in private.log; less urgent private levels are checked even when absent from the displayed samples.

practice.title: Test what none excludes
practice.action: Remove ;authpriv.none from the general line and run, then restore it.
practice.observe: The same authpriv record now leaks to both logs; none affected only the line where it was written.

review.introduction: Explains that a later private rule cannot undo a general-log copy; teaches same-rule none exclusions and all authpriv levels, separating routing from permissions.
review.example: Actual sample includes private alert and debug events, so the learner sees both general-log leakage and dropped private detail before repairing the separate practice configuration.
review.assignment: Independent private/general routing is graded across every facility/severity combination, including absence from wrong destinations; no complete solved configuration is exposed by default.

worked.label: Worked configuration
worked.explanation: Different sample policy: Exclude one source from a broad rule while retaining its private records.

concepts.title: Sensitive records need a separate destination
concepts.text: authpriv labels private authentication events. If *.notice writes a general log, authpriv events still match it. A later private-log line does not undo the earlier general-log copy.

concepts.title: Exclude from the same selector
concepts.text: The worked selector *.notice;authpriv.none removes authpriv from that general rule. The semicolon joins selectors for one destination; none means no levels for the named facility in that rule.

concepts.title: Keep all private levels deliberately
concepts.text: authpriv.* selects every severity for the private log, including debug7. A threshold such as authpriv.notice would lose less urgent private records. Permissions and storage protection of real private logs need separate administration; this task models routing only.

goal: Combine thresholds, exact reports and exclusions in a whole-policy handover.
requirements: Route authpriv levels0–7 once to /var/log/private.log.
Route every other facility at notice(5) or more urgent once to /var/log/operations.log.
Also route daemon and cron events at exactly info(6) once to /var/log/service.log.
Deliver nothing else; no duplicate copies are permitted.

practice.title: Trace each required destination
practice.action: Read the three practice requirements above the editor. Identify the broad threshold, private stream and exact mail.notice report.
practice.observe: One broad selector cannot express all three policies; the routes have different source and level sets.

practice.title: Repair the complete policy
practice.action: Run routing test on the starter. Edit each relevant line or Insert worked configuration, then run again.
practice.observe: Actual delivery rows show the sample event paths; outcome feedback checks the full source/severity space.

practice.title: Diagnose a duplicate without losing coverage
practice.action: Duplicate the operations rule and run. Remove only the extra copy, then rerun.
practice.observe: Removing both copies would lose events. The requirement is exactly one delivery, not at least one.

review.introduction: Combines different destination/source/level policies and comma grouping only when levels match; demonstrates a different full sample before the independent handover.
review.example: Guides complete policy repair and deliberate duplicate creation/removal, using extra mail notice/service warning samples; actual replay and full-matrix feedback remain distinct.
review.assignment: Full editor task preserves private coverage, the specified general threshold and two-source exact stream; equivalent supported rules, order, case and comments pass without relaxing copies.

worked.label: Worked configuration
worked.explanation: Different sample policy: Combine thresholds, exact reports and exclusions in a whole-policy handover.

concepts.title: Translate each destination into its own rule
concepts.text: Start from the required destination, source set and level set. In the worked policy, operations needs non-private warnings and more urgent events; private needs all authpriv levels; service needs only mail.notice.

concepts.title: Combine facilities only when their level policy matches
concepts.text: A comma shares one level selection across facilities: daemon,cron.=info selects exactly info from both. It does not mean all daemon levels plus cron info. Use separate lines when the policies differ.

concepts.title: Validate the whole handover
concepts.text: Extra broad rules can leak private records or duplicate deliveries even after another rule looks correct. Test the starter, inspect specific mismatches, remove redundant routes, then retest all destinations. Comments and reordered equivalent rules are accepted.

goal: Keep maintenance state separate from startup policy.
requirements: Kiln is entering a maintenance window. Change current availability and future enrollment independently. Keep kiln-app.service stopped during maintenance, but enroll it in kiln.target for the next session.
Run kiln-inspection.service at virtual port 9200 now, but remove its startup link so it stays stopped next session.
Keep kiln-observer.service running at 9100 now and next session. Preserve all supplied files, other links and the default target.

practice.title: Inspect the supplied plan
practice.action: Run systemctl status sketchplan-app.service, systemctl is-enabled sketchplan-app.service and systemctl get-default in the example terminal.
practice.observe: Compare current runtime with startup enrollment and the next-session target before editing.

practice.title: Apply the worked policy
practice.action: Run the explained Stop, Enable, Start and Disable commands in the example terminal. Check both sessions.
practice.observe: Save, manager reload, current program state and next-session policy have separate effects.

practice.title: Break only the future policy
practice.action: After the example passes, run systemctl disable sketchplan-app.service. Its current status does not change, but next-session application coverage fails. Enable it again and recheck.
practice.observe: Identify the failed next-session rows while comparing the unchanged current service status. Repair and recheck.

worked.label: App now / next time
worked.explanation: Stop and Enable affect separate parts of the model.

worked.label: Inspection now / next time
worked.explanation: Start and Disable can both be correct for the same service.

concepts.title: Two independent questions
concepts.text: A service is a program controlled by a service manager. Active asks whether a service is running now. Enabled asks whether startup links request it later. Starting does not enable; enabling does not start. A stopped service can be enabled, and a running one can be disabled.

concepts.title: Read evidence before applying policy
concepts.text: In the worked sketchplan system, use systemctl status sketchplan-app.service and systemctl is-enabled sketchplan-app.service. Read the result, not just a success line from an earlier command. systemctl cat sketchplan-app.service shows the saved WantedBy target. Virtual ports are labels; nothing listens on this computer.

concepts.title: A maintenance plan
concepts.text: The worked plan keeps sketchplan-app.service stopped now but enabled for next time, while sketchplan-inspection.service runs only now. Stop the app and enable it. Start inspection, then disable its startup enrollment. A Check also starts a separate copy from the saved default; it does not change the current practice system.

goal: Choose the next target without switching the current session.
requirements: The host is currently in a maintenance session, but the next start must use its normal service group. Select harbor.target for the next session; it must start only that target, harbor-app.service at 8443 and harbor-observer.service at 9100.
Keep the current harbor-maintenance.target, harbor-app.service, harbor-inspection.service at 9200 and harbor-observer.service at 9100 active. Do not start harbor.target now.
Remove harbor-inspection.service from harbor-maintenance.target startup enrollment. Preserve every file and every other install link.

practice.title: Inspect the supplied plan
practice.action: Run systemctl status galleryplan-app.service, systemctl is-enabled galleryplan-app.service and systemctl get-default in the example terminal.
practice.observe: Compare current runtime with startup enrollment and the next-session target before editing.

practice.title: Apply the worked policy
practice.action: Run the explained Disable and Set-default commands. Use Get-default and Status to inspect the result before Check.
practice.observe: Save, manager reload, current program state and next-session policy have separate effects.

practice.title: Break only the future policy
practice.action: After the example passes, run systemctl set-default galleryplan-maintenance.target. Current services stay unchanged but next-session results fail. Restore galleryplan.target with set-default and check again.
practice.observe: Identify the failed next-session rows while comparing the unchanged current service status. Repair and recheck.

worked.label: Current target
worked.explanation: Remains active; no switch or reboot is performed.

worked.label: Selected next target
worked.explanation: The separate next-session check follows this target’s startup links.

worked.label: Inspection
worked.explanation: Disabling removes enrollment, not the running program.

concepts.title: A target groups services
concepts.text: A target is a named group requested by the manager. Enabling a service adds a link to the target named by WantedBy. A link in one target does not make a different default target request that service.

concepts.title: Next time is different from now
concepts.text: Use systemctl get-default in the worked galleryplan system. systemctl set-default galleryplan.target changes the next-session choice; it does not stop galleryplan-maintenance.target, start the new target or change current services. This is not systemctl isolate, which is outside this simulator.

concepts.title: Observe both sessions
concepts.text: The worked policy keeps current inspection running, removes its maintenance startup link and selects galleryplan.target for next time. Check inspects a separate next-session copy. Current maintenance remains active while the copy starts only the normal target, application and observer.

goal: Move startup enrollment without leaving an old target link.
requirements: The application is enrolled in the wrong service group. Repair its installation metadata and actual enrollment; editing WantedBy alone does not move existing links. Enroll press-app.service in press.target, remove its old press-maintenance.target link and select press.target for next time.
Keep press-app.service running at 8443 using its current saved and loaded definition. Keep press-inspection.service running at 9200 now but absent next session.

Keep press-observer.service running at 9100 now and next time. Preserve every application configuration, other unit documents and all other install links. The next session must start only press.target, press-app.service and press-observer.service.

practice.action: Run systemctl status proofplan-app.service, systemctl is-enabled proofplan-app.service and systemctl get-default in the example terminal.
practice.observe: Compare current runtime with startup enrollment and the next-session target before editing.

practice.title: Apply the worked policy
practice.action: Edit the app’s WantedBy in the unit editor and Save. Run the explained disable/reload/enable/default and stop/start sequence, then inspect current source and Check.
practice.observe: Save, manager reload, current program state and next-session policy have separate effects.

practice.title: Break only the future policy
practice.action: After the example passes, run systemctl disable proofplan-app.service. Its current status does not change, but next-session application coverage fails. Enable it again and recheck.
practice.observe: Identify the failed next-session rows while comparing the unchanged current service status. Repair and recheck.

worked.label: Saved WantedBy
worked.explanation: Change only this app’s install target.

worked.label: Enrollment
worked.value: proofplan.target: app present; proofplan-maintenance.target: app absent
worked.explanation: Disable removes old links; Enable uses the saved installation metadata.

worked.label: Current app
worked.explanation: Reload and current execution are separate checks.

concepts.title: Instructions and installed links differ
concepts.text: WantedBy in [Install] tells Enable where to create a startup link. It is not itself an active dependency. Changing that text and reloading the manager do not remove links created earlier. Inspect the saved text and actual enrollment separately.

concepts.title: Move an enrollment deliberately
concepts.text: In the different proofplan system, disable proofplan-app.service to remove its old enrollment. In the editor change its WantedBy to proofplan.target, Save, and run systemctl daemon-reload. Enable creates the new link. Select proofplan.target as the next default. Other service links must remain untouched.

concepts.title: Loaded and running versions
concepts.text: This task also requires the app’s current run to use the edited source. Reload reads saved definitions but does not replace a running program. Stop and start only proofplan-app.service, then inspect status and the loaded/current inputs. All configuration values stay unchanged. Check independently verifies current work and the next-session group.

goal: Prepare an Ethernet profile for the next startup.
context: Builds on the Linux host addressing and route lessons. Learn saved-profile editing before planning startup preference or a two-uplink handover.

concepts.title: Saved settings are not current settings
concepts.text: A connection profile is a named set of saved network settings. A UUID identifies that profile; interface-name binds it to an adapter. Editing a saved file does not rewrite the settings already in use.

concepts.title: Give a wired adapter its next settings
concepts.text: Under [ipv4], method=manual selects a supplied static address. address1 combines an IPv4 address and prefix. gateway is the on-link next hop for other networks. Under [connection], autoconnect=true makes the saved profile eligible when its adapter is free.

concepts.title: Read both observations
concepts.text: Test startup profiles validates virtual files, re-reads them without replacing current selections, then separately models a fresh startup. Current settings and Next startup are different observations. The task is not asking you to interrupt the running connection.

worked.label: Profile identity and adapter
worked.explanation: Keep the supplied UUID. Bind this worked profile to an existing adapter and make it eligible when that adapter is free.

worked.label: Static workshop settings
worked.explanation: The prefix defines the local network; the gateway is the supplied on-link next hop. These values belong only to the separate workshop.

worked.label: Observation
worked.value:
Re-read → keep current
Startup → use edited profile
worked.explanation: The test displays both results. Saving a profile is not the same action as replacing current interface settings.

requirements: Prepare the saved Application profile for the next simulated startup: bind it to enp1s0, enable automatic selection and give it 10.70.0.20/24.
Reach 172.16.5.10 through enp1s0, the preferred default uplink, in both supplied cases.
Re-reading saved profiles must preserve the current management settings.
Retain supplied filenames and UUIDs.

practice.title: Find and test the saved settings
practice.action: Choose app.nmconnection and Test startup profiles. Compare Current settings with Next startup.
practice.observe: The current connection can be correct while the saved starter would fail at a later startup.

practice.title: Repair the workshop profile
practice.action: In app.nmconnection, set interface-name=enp1s0, autoconnect=true and address1=10.80.0.20/24, or Insert worked profiles. Test startup profiles.
practice.observe: Both supplied cases should pass. Read the actual next-startup address and selected profile.

practice.title: Exclude and restore the profile
practice.action: Change Application to autoconnect=false, test again, then restore true and retest.
practice.observe: A valid saved address is not enough when its profile is ineligible.

goal: Retire a stale startup preference without interrupting the current link.
context: Builds on the Linux host addressing and route lessons. Learn saved-profile editing before planning startup preference or a two-uplink handover.

concepts.title: Two profiles can name one adapter
concepts.text: Only one saved Ethernet profile is selected per supplied adapter at startup. A higher autoconnect-priority is preferred. A filename or friendly name does not decide which wins.

concepts.title: Fix the next selection without replacing the current one
concepts.text: Re-reading changed profile files does not preempt a connection already selected. In this practice, Old Application remains current, while the next-startup result should choose Replacement. Inspect the UUID as well as its name.

concepts.title: Avoid ambiguous ties
concepts.text: You can raise the replacement priority, lower the old priority, or set the old autoconnect=false. A real tie can depend on activation history; this bounded simulator refuses ties instead of pretending alphabetical order is correct.

worked.label: Competing saved profiles
worked.explanation: Both are eligible for the same supplied adapter. A higher number is preferred; friendly names and filenames do not choose the winner.

worked.label: Worked replacement preference
worked.explanation: In Replacement, 30 outranks Old Application’s 20. Lowering the old preference or excluding it from autoconnect is another supported approach.

worked.label: Current versus next
worked.value:
Current: Old Application UUID
Next startup: Replacement UUID
worked.explanation: Editing/re-reading saved files does not preempt an already selected profile. Use Selection details to inspect the full identities.

requirements: Make the supplied Replacement profile (00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000074) win automatic selection on enp1s0 at the next startup.
It must provide 10.72.0.20/24 and the usable application path to 172.16.5.10; enp1s0 remains the preferred default uplink.
Re-reading files must keep BOTH current interface settings unchanged.
Retain all supplied filenames and UUIDs.
Do not rely on a priority tie.

practice.title: Find the competing profiles
practice.action: Select app.nmconnection and replacement.nmconnection. Compare their priorities, then Test startup profiles.
practice.observe: The higher-priority stale saved profile wins next startup even though current settings remain unchanged.

practice.title: Prefer the replacement
practice.action: Change Replacement’s priority to 30, or Insert worked profiles, then Test startup profiles.
practice.observe: Replacement wins the next-startup selection; the current UUID remains Old Application.

practice.title: Observe a tie honestly
practice.action: Set Replacement’s priority to 20 and test. Then restore 30 and retry.
practice.observe: A tied preference reports unsupported history-dependent selection, rather than inventing a filename winner.

goal: Keep management access while changing the next default uplink.
context: Builds on the Linux host addressing and route lessons. Learn saved-profile editing before planning startup preference or a two-uplink handover.

concepts.title: Profile preference and route preference are different
concepts.text: autoconnect-priority chooses a profile for one adapter. Once adapters are configured, routes choose where traffic leaves. The longest destination prefix wins; among equal-length routes, a lower route metric wins.

concepts.title: Give management a specific path
concepts.text: An application default route can coexist with a more specific management route. route1=NETWORK/PREFIX,GATEWAY,METRIC describes a numeric route in this subset. The gateway must be on that adapter’s local network.

concepts.title: Keep automatic defaults explicit in your reasoning
concepts.text: An omitted or -1 metric uses the supplied per-interface automatic value. The two test cases deliberately supply different values. never-default=true prevents that profile from contributing a default route; it does not create a management route. Unsupported policy combinations are reported honestly.

worked.label: Application default
worked.explanation: An explicit lower metric makes the application default preferred to the management default. This is route preference, not autoconnect priority.

worked.label: Management destination
worked.explanation: This worked option omits Management’s default and supplies its specific path. A more specific destination wins before route metrics are compared.

worked.label: Two sample contexts
worked.value:
A: app 100 / management 200
B: app 600 / management 100
worked.explanation: Omitted/-1 metrics use these sample inputs. Explicit supported policy must satisfy both contexts; they are not a claim about every real host’s defaults.

requirements: Prepare a two-uplink handover: at next startup enp1s0 (10.74.0.20/24) is the preferred default and reaches 172.16.5.10.
Reach the management destination 10.40.0.50 through enp2s0 via its supplied gateway 10.75.0.1 in both metric contexts.
Re-reading files must preserve current management settings.
Retain supplied filenames and UUIDs; use supported explicit routes/metrics or never-default policy without metric ties.

practice.title: Inspect both destinations
practice.action: Test startup profiles and read which interface is selected for the application and management destinations.
practice.observe: A working management default can send application traffic through the wrong uplink.

practice.title: Build the workshop handover
practice.action: Insert worked profiles, select management.nmconnection and read never-default and route1. Test startup profiles.
practice.observe: Application’s default and Management’s longer-prefix route handle different destinations; current management remains unchanged.

practice.title: Remove and restore the specific route
practice.action: Remove route1 from Management and test, then restore it and retry.
practice.observe: Suppressing Management’s default does not create a management path. The route requirement must still be met.

goal: Prepare required project storage and optional audit media, then prove both successful mounts and meaningful missing-media failures.
context: Builds on disk/filesystem identity. This configuration task uses the supplied filesystem inventory; no actual device preparation or restart is required.

concepts.title: A saved row requests a mount
concepts.text: A mount makes a filesystem available at a directory. The six fields name its source, directory, filesystem type, options, dump frequency and check order. UUID identifies the filesystem even when its /dev alias changes. Copy the supplied filesystem type; this task does not format media. The final two numbers are supplied; this task records them without assessing backup or filesystem-check ordering.

concepts.title: Automatic, optional and read-only mean different things
concepts.text: auto requests a mount automatically and is the default; noauto leaves it out of this table’s automatic requests. nofail makes an automatic request optional for the modeled local-filesystem target. It does not skip the request, make a failed filesystem mount, or guarantee the optional medium is ready by a deadline. ro controls write access; rw allows writes.

concepts.title: Keep required storage failures visible
concepts.text: In the workshop, /workshop is required and /media/camera is optional. Test both-present, camera-absent and workshop-absent samples. A missing camera may leave an optional mount failed while required checks succeed. A missing required workshop filesystem must remain a problem. The task checks that distinction; a correct requirement check is not a claim the whole system booted.

worked.label: Required workshop options
worked.explanation: Keep the workshop automatic and required. Losing it must remain visible; defaults or rw with implicit auto also work in this subset.

worked.label: Optional camera options
worked.explanation: Request the camera automatically and read-only, while allowing required checks to succeed if it is absent.

worked.label: Read the actual outcome
worked.explanation: The all-present sample must still show the intended camera volume mounted read-only. Readiness alone cannot prove a correct UUID or type.

requirements: Configure only /project and /media/audit using the supplied intended filesystems.
Make /project a required automatic read/write mount, and /media/audit an optional automatic read-only mount.
Both correct volumes must mount when available.
If only the removable audit medium is absent, required-storage checks must still succeed.
If the project filesystem is absent, its required-storage problem must remain visible.
Do not hide that failure with nofail or skip the requested automatic mounts with noauto.

practice.title: Inspect the starting requests
practice.action: Choose Run mount checks, then compare the three Supplied samples. Read both the requirement checks and Actual mount attempts.
practice.observe: The starter makes workshop storage optional and skips the camera automatically. A skipped request differs from an optional request that was attempted.

practice.title: Repair the workshop policy
practice.action: In the editor, use rw,auto for /workshop and ro,auto,nofail for /media/camera, keeping the supplied UUIDs and types. You may Insert worked policy. Run mount checks.
practice.observe: All sample requirements should be met. The workshop-absent sample must still show a failed required mount; that expected protection is separate from passing the task checks.

practice.title: Try hiding a required failure
practice.action: Add nofail to /workshop and Run mount checks. Read the required-storage failure feedback, then remove that nofail and retry.
practice.observe: Making every request optional can conceal missing workshop storage. A table that can proceed is not necessarily the table the task requires.

goal: Repair local records without breaking unrelated names.
context: Builds on the Linux host resolver lesson. Edit only these two virtual file excerpts; all DNS answers and availability are supplied sample inputs.

concepts.title: One line can give a computer several names
concepts.text: A hosts file is a local address book. Put the dotted-decimal address first, then the main name and any short aliases, separated by spaces. All names on that row refer to the same address. A # begins a comment. Editing this activity changes only simulated files.

concepts.title: Keep the names you still need
concepts.text: To repair an address, change its row without damaging neighboring rows. To retire an alias, remove only that name. Keep the main name and its replacement alias. Case does not change the meaning of a name in this subset; duplicate names across rows are rejected rather than guessed.

concepts.title: Check the application’s lookup, not just the text
concepts.text: The supplied hosts: files dns row means try the local table first, then the DNS sample if the name is missing locally. A successful local answer stops the search. Inspect the actual source trace after Run lookups. Here localhost and the camera remain local, including when DNS is unavailable.

worked.label: Short alias
worked.explanation: The studio alias shares the address of studio.workshop.lab.test because both names are on that hosts row.

worked.label: Retired name
worked.explanation: Remove the name, not the unrelated camera or localhost rows.

worked.label: Observe the trace
worked.explanation: The local answer is returned before any supplied DNS lookup.

requirements: Give dispatch.office.lab.test and the short alias dispatch the supplied local address 192.0.2.55.
Remove the retired alias old-dispatch.
Preserve localhost at 127.0.0.1 and printer.office.lab.test at 192.0.2.60.
Prove these local answers work with DNS available and unavailable.

practice.title: Read the current local row
practice.action: Choose hosts in File. Choose Run lookups and compare studio.workshop.lab.test, studio and old-studio.
practice.observe: The starter has the old address and retired alias. The main name may resolve, but a successful answer can still be the wrong address.

practice.title: Repair only the intended row
practice.action: Set the studio row to 198.51.100.35 studio.workshop.lab.test studio, remove old-studio, and keep the localhost/camera rows. Choose Run lookups. Insert worked configuration can fill the separate practice files without running them.
practice.observe: All five lookups meet their requirements in both samples. DNS being unavailable does not prevent a valid local hosts answer.

practice.title: Explore an alias safely
practice.action: Change studio to studio-old in the hosts row and Run lookups. Read the missing-name feedback, then restore studio and retry.
practice.observe: The main name still works while the requested short alias does not. One passing name cannot prove every required alias is correct.

goal: Keep intentional local overrides while preserving useful DNS fallback.
context: Builds on the Linux host resolver lesson. Edit only these two virtual file excerpts; all DNS answers and availability are supplied sample inputs.

concepts.title: The source order chooses which answer wins
concepts.text: Applications using the name-service switch follow the hosts: row from left to right. files reads the local hosts table; dns asks the supplied DNS sample here. A successful source normally returns immediately. If both know a name, placing files first gives a deliberate local override priority. Here nsswitch.conf shows only its hosts row; a real file also has other database settings.

concepts.title: Missing and unavailable are different outcomes
concepts.text: NOTFOUND means the source was consulted but has no matching name. UNAVAIL means the source cannot be used in that sample. Both normally continue to the next source. SUCCESS normally returns the answer. Bracket rules follow the source they control: files [NOTFOUND=return] dns stops a missing local name before DNS can be tried.

concepts.title: Verify fallback without copying a remote address
concepts.text: A hosts entry is static. DNS answers can change between samples, so copying one catalog address into hosts is not a repair. Keep the local override and peer local, let missing names reach DNS, and inspect the outage/unavailable-table traces. A lookup that has no answer must remain visibly unresolved.

worked.label: Local override first
worked.explanation: A successful local match returns; otherwise the next source is consulted.

worked.label: Successful local lookup
worked.explanation: Keep the deliberate studio override instead of accepting stale DNS.

worked.label: A name absent locally
worked.explanation: With no local match, continue to DNS; its successful catalog answer is returned. The complete status words appear in the actual trace.

worked.label: A source cannot be used
worked.explanation: Try the next supported source; this is different from finding no name in a working source.

requirements: Prefer the local override rescue.office.lab.test and alias rescue at 192.0.2.55; preserve printer.office.lab.test at 192.0.2.60.
Resolve catalog.office.lab.test through the supplied DNS snapshot, not a copied local address.
Let a missing local name continue to DNS.
Keep the override working during a DNS outage.
If the local table is unavailable, use the supplied DNS backup for the override and report the peer honestly as unresolved.

practice.title: Investigate which source stops the lookup
practice.action: Choose Run lookups. Select each Supplied DNS sample and inspect the studio override, catalog and camera traces.
practice.observe: The starter asks DNS first and its return-on-miss/outage rules can prevent local fallback. Read the actual status and action, not just the final address.

practice.title: Apply the default fallback policy
practice.action: Choose nsswitch.conf in File. Use hosts: files dns, leaving the studio/camera hosts rows intact, then Run lookups. Insert worked configuration fills practice files but does not run them.
practice.observe: Local studio wins over stale DNS. The catalog follows changing DNS snapshots. DNS outage and unavailable-local-table samples exercise different fallback paths.

practice.title: See why return-on-miss blocks DNS
practice.action: Use hosts: files [NOTFOUND=return] dns in the practice nsswitch.conf and Run lookups. Find the failing catalog traces, then restore hosts: files dns and retry.
practice.observe: A missing local catalog name now stops at files instead of reaching DNS. The local override still passes: retain those correct individual results while repairing fallback.

goal: Choose the intended site while retaining useful search fallback.
context: Builds on local-name/source-order practice. This resolver excerpt controls only search settings; DNS answers and the sample hostname are supplied inputs. These queries have already reached DNS; local hosts entries are outside this activity.

concepts.title: A short name needs context
concepts.text: DNS stores complete names such as preview.studio.workshop.lab.test. A search list lets a relative name such as preview try a suffix. search studio.workshop.lab.test archive.workshop.lab.test tries those sites in that order. A positive answer stops the search, even if it belongs to the wrong site.

concepts.title: A missing name can fall through

concepts.title: Attaching a filesystem is separate from opening its files
concepts.text: Mounting attaches a supplied filesystem at a directory called its mountpoint. This lesson uses simulated media only. Permission to mount does not change ownership or access permissions inside the mounted filesystem. The administrator is a separate privileged caller; the two named operators are ordinary callers.

concepts.title: Choose who may end an ordinary session
concepts.text: user permits any ordinary operator to mount the configured entry. Among ordinary operators, only its actual mounter can unmount it. It is not a setting that names Alex or another account. With neither user nor users, mounting requires the administrator. In this lab, requesting an already-mounted volume is a no-op; it does not change its actual mounter. Real Linux also supports stacked mounts, which this exercise excludes.

concepts.title: Read options in order
concepts.text: The fourth field of each six-field entry contains comma-separated options. ro selects read-only mounting and noauto keeps the entry out of this table’s startup requests. user and users also imply noexec, nosuid and nodev. A later exec, suid or dev can undo the corresponding restriction. We inspect these policy flags; this simulator does not execute files, set-user-ID programs or device nodes.

concepts.title: Saved policy and the current mount are different
concepts.text: Save configuration updates the simulated table. It does not remount a filesystem, replace its actual mounter or rewrite already-applied flags. Inspect Current mounts, then use the proper caller to unmount and mount again when a task requires changed live options. Current saved policy controls ordinary unmount authorization.

concepts.title: Check the task as well as other callers
concepts.text: Use the caller and mountpoint selectors for hands-on operations. Check work verifies your actual session and tries the saved policy against separate supplied cases. Each case starts with its own sample media and callers; those checks leave your current session unchanged. A missing medium stays missing even if its entry permits ordinary mounting.
