goal: Repair filesystem bookkeeping offline while preserving access and data.
context: Builds on inodes, hard links, device names and mounting non-root filesystems. All supplied devices and files are simulated.

concepts.title: A filename points to stored file information
concepts.text: A directory entry associates a name with an inode: the file record that refers to its contents and data blocks. Two hard links can name the same inode. The stored link count should equal the number of names.

concepts.title: Allocation records can disagree with the files
concepts.text: A filesystem also records which blocks and inode slots are in use, plus totals of free space. These are bookkeeping records, not the file contents themselves. A checker compares them with actual references; a wrong free-space total is not proof that bytes have vanished.

concepts.title: Inspect, unmount, then check the supplied device
concepts.text: findmnt shows which virtual device belongs to which mountpoint. Unmount only the repair target. e2fsck -fn DEVICE forces a read-only check: -f means check even if marked clean; -n means answer no to changes. This exercise refuses all checks on mounted volumes because real mounted check results are unreliable and mounted repair is unsafe.

concepts.title: Choose an appropriate repair and verify it
concepts.text: e2fsck -fp DEVICE applies supported safe automatic repairs (-p, preen). Exit status 1 means corrections were made, not a command syntax error. Status 4 means findings remain; 5 means both corrections and remaining findings. Run -fn again, restore the supplied mount, and check the file contents. Real maintenance requires backups and a device-specific recovery plan.

concepts.title: Keep checking and changing separate
concepts.text: dumpe2fs -h DEVICE shows the stored summary, which can be wrong. ls -li shows names, inode numbers and link counts. Neither query repairs anything. The lesson uses an abstract ext-family graph, not a raw ext4 image or a recovery guarantee. Use help for the exact supported command subset.

goal: Recover retained unnamed file data without confusing automatic repair with an explicit decision.
context: Builds on inodes, hard links, device names and mounting non-root filesystems. All supplied devices and files are simulated.

concepts.title: Build on the offline accounting repair
concepts.text: The previous lesson separated filenames, inode records and data blocks. Keep the same safe sequence: inspect the supplied mounts, unmount only the target, diagnose with e2fsck -fn, then recheck and remount after repair. Preen corrects supported accounting; it does not authorize every recovery decision. Status 1 means corrected, 4 means findings remain, and 5 means both.

concepts.title: An unnamed file can still contain retained data
concepts.text: An unattached inode has retained contents but no directory name. Preen does not decide to reconnect a nonempty file. In this bounded, known exercise, e2fsck -fy DEVICE explicitly authorizes modeled recovery (-y, yes) and attaches it under lost+found. It is not safe advice to blindly answer yes on an unknown real disk.

concepts.title: Inspect recovered content, not a guessed filename
concepts.text: ls -li MOUNTPOINT/lost+found shows each recovered inode and its chosen name. An occupied #inode name causes a suffix. Use cat on the actual reported name; do not assume a particular inode number or discard an unexpected file. Multiple supplied samples check retained content and collision handling.

worked.label: Find the target
worked.explanation: Read the device-to-mount association and the report inode before making changes. The separate example-notes volume is protected.

worked.label: Check offline
worked.explanation: Expected: derived consistency findings and status 4; actual output appears only after Run command.

worked.label: Repair accounting
worked.explanation: Expected in this first workshop: status 4, with retained unnamed data requiring a decision. Preen leaves that file unrecovered. Status 5 means earlier corrections were made but findings still remain; read the actual report.

worked.label: Authorize retained-data recovery
worked.explanation: Only this known exercise authorizes explicit recovery. Retained contents are reconnected under lost+found; missing/overwritten bytes cannot be invented.

worked.label: Verify and restore access
worked.explanation: Expected: no remaining findings (status 0), then the original report or recovered names. Use cat on a listed recovered file to inspect its actual contents.

concepts.title: Startup files prepare a shell
concepts.text: A login shell is Bash started for a login, or with --login; it may read settings before you type. Interactive means a person can type commands; login describes how it was started. Not every terminal window is a login shell. This activity explicitly labels each supplied session.

concepts.title: Bash chooses the first personal login file
concepts.text: After /etc/profile, a login Bash checks ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, then ~/.profile. It reads the first present, readable personal file, not all three. An empty .bash_profile still wins; it does not make Bash fall through. Here every supplied file is readable.

concepts.title: Apply values in the file that runs
concepts.text: The system profile creates and exports BASE from the supplied SITE. Keep it. In the worked example WORKSHOP is supplied, while TOOL_LABEL is your new value. TOOL_LABEL="$WORKSHOP-tool" joins the supplied value to -tool; export TOOL_LABEL lets a new program receive it. LOCAL_NOTE stays in the login shell without export.

concepts.title: A terminal window and a script start differently
concepts.text: An interactive shell is waiting for a person to type commands. A non-login interactive Bash reads ~/.bashrc. A noninteractive Bash runs a script; it does not automatically read .bashrc. A greeting useful to a person can corrupt a script’s output.

concepts.title: A script may have a selected settings file
concepts.text: For Bash, BASH_ENV can select a startup file for a noninteractive invocation. This lesson supplies that selection: /work/startup.env or none. It is not a file you must create on your computer. With no selected file, the supplied setting stays as it was.

concepts.title: Separate a greeting from shared settings
concepts.text: In the worked example WORKSHOP is supplied. TOOL_LABEL is created from it and exported for the new program. Put the Ready greeting only in .bashrc; put the quiet setting in the selected script-startup file. printf prints text; export shares a value, without printing it.

concepts.title: A package default is not always your active setting
concepts.text: A conffile is a configuration file that the package manager treats specially. Compare three versions: the previous packaged default, the local file used at this site, and the incoming packaged default. A program upgrade and a configuration decision are related but different outcomes.

concepts.title: Use the comparison before choosing
concepts.text: An untouched local file can follow a changed package default automatically. A local-only edit remains when the package default has not changed. Identical local and incoming text needs no choice. When both differ from the previous default and from each other, choose deliberately. The native review labels these cases; a review alone changes no files.

concepts.title: Keep a review copy or a recovery copy

goal: Use file purpose to repair a stopped application’s configuration, reference data, persistent state and log locations.
requirements: Beacon is stopped. Work as Alex in the supplied delegated Beacon subfolders; parent hierarchy folders remain protected.

Place the host settings, locally installed read-only reference, persistent changing progress and event log into their corresponding Beacon folders under /etc, /usr/local/share, /var/lib and /var/log. Keep each original filename.
Finish with exactly the appropriate one file in each of the four Beacon folders; remove the wrong-location copies without losing their text.
Keep every /work/intake original’s text and mode, the private note’s text and mode, and /etc/site-policy.txt unchanged.
Investigate with the simulated terminal, make the file changes and choose Check work.

concepts.title: Choose a directory by the file’s job
concepts.text: A configuration file tells a program what to do. A reference table is input that the program reads without updating. A checkpoint remembers changing work between runs. A log records events. A familiar-looking filename is a clue, not proof: use cat to read the supplied small text files.

concepts.title: Four locations, four purposes
concepts.text: For this site, /etc/APP holds host configuration; /usr/local/share/APP holds locally installed reference data that is not tied to a particular kind of processor; /var/lib/APP holds persistent changing state; /var/log/APP holds event logs. APP means the application’s own folder. This is not a rule that every local program must use /etc: /usr/local/etc is also a valid local configuration location.

concepts.title: Relocate safely
concepts.text: mv SOURCE DESTINATION changes a file’s location; cp leaves the source in place. Here the application is stopped and Alex may change its application folders. Root-owned parent folders remain protected. This is a supplied training arrangement, not permission to rearrange a running service or system folders on a real computer.

concepts.title: Verify the files, not just the command
concepts.text: A silent mv usually means success. List each application folder and inspect its text. Retain the separate intake originals and private note. The reference files are called read-only data because the application does not update them; that description does not mean their permissions can never allow an administrator to replace them.

context: You have practised paths, cat, single-file cp/mv and quoted find patterns. Type in the simulated terminal and choose Run. Alex has permission only in the supplied app/work folders; do not use sudo.

practice.observe: Each correct application folder receives its matching file; its wrong-location copy disappears. The independent originals remain in /work/demo-originals.

concepts.title: Start with the directory’s purpose
concepts.text: Host configuration belongs in this site’s /etc application folder. Local reference data is under /usr/local/share, persistent progress under /var/lib, and events under /var/log. A support copy in /work is a handover copy; it does not change the application’s own configuration or installation.

concepts.title: Find candidates, then inspect the relationship
concepts.text: find /etc -type f -name 'site.conf' lists matching ordinary files below one starting folder. Quote patterns such as '*.conf'. find matches paths, not file contents: cat the active application’s configuration to learn which reference, checkpoint and event files it actually names. Archived and neighbouring files can have the same filename.

concepts.title: Keep originals and name the handover clearly
concepts.text: cp SOURCE DESTINATION copies one ordinary file without moving its source. The four requested handover names describe their roles. A checkpoint is not an event log; an archived file is not current just because its name matches. Check source paths and text before making each copy.

concepts.title: Inspect after a change
concepts.text: ls -a reveals extra hidden handover files as well as ordinary names. cat checks the copied text. Inspect the finished handover and confirm the originals are still in place. Several command sequences can reach that result.

goal: Investigate endpoint ownership, retire one obsolete listener and preserve a same-name local instance plus approved services.
requirements: You are Alex in a supplied virtual process and IPv4 endpoint inventory. Investigate numeric TCP/UDP endpoints and their owning processes; a command name alone is not enough to choose the right instance.
Retire the obsolete preview listener bound to TCP 0.0.0.0:8081: that endpoint must be closed and its owning process ended. Do not merely pause it or leave a termination request waiting.
Keep the separate preview instance bound to TCP 127.0.0.1:8082 unchanged. Keep the approved TCP 192.0.2.10:8443 and UDP 127.0.0.1:5353 endpoints bound as well.

Preserve every unrelated process, including init and both sessions: retain its owner, parent, command name, activity/paused state and nice value. The approved endpoint owners must remain unchanged and active; bound alone does not mean a paused application is usable.
This is a runtime retirement only. A wildcard bind covers local interfaces, not proof of Internet reachability; no real network, firewall or next-boot service policy is tested.

Type commands in the simulated terminal and choose Run. Inspect the resulting endpoints and process states, then choose Check work. Correct partial work and retry; equivalent supported ways of ending only the unwanted instance are accepted.
context: Builds on PID selection, signals and Linux host addresses. You type one supported command into the simulated terminal and choose Run; command names are not a real shell. Practice uses Morgan and a different endpoint set. The assignment uses Alex; both have their own saved command and transcript.

concepts.title: An endpoint identifies where a program accepts traffic
concepts.text: An endpoint combines a protocol, local address and port number. TCP and UDP are different protocols even when a port number matches. In these supplied IPv4 facts, 127.0.0.1 is loopback-only; 0.0.0.0 means a bind on all local IPv4 interfaces. It does not prove that another computer or the Internet can reach the program. The process ID, or PID, identifies which instance owns the endpoint.

concepts.title: Read the numeric socket view
concepts.text: ss -lntup lists the supplied listening TCP and unconnected UDP endpoints. -l selects these listener/bound rows, -n keeps addresses and ports numeric, -t includes TCP, -u includes UDP and -p requests process details. TCP shows LISTEN; the modeled unconnected UDP endpoint shows UNCONN and is still bound. ss -lntp selects only TCP; ss -lnup only UDP. The lab simulates this supported subset of real ss options entirely in memory.

concepts.title: Match the PID, not just the name
concepts.text: Two instances can have the same command name while serving different addresses or ports. Read the needed endpoint row and relate its PID to ps before choosing an action. Alex can see every supplied endpoint, but -p only shows process details for Alex’s own processes; another owner’s blank process column does not mean the endpoint is absent. The model also permits a simulated root view, but no identity change is needed here.

concepts.title: Pausing keeps the socket open
concepts.text: STOP pauses a process; it does not close its endpoints. CONT lets it continue. In this supplied process model, TERM on an active process ends it; TERM received while paused waits until CONT. KILL ends it immediately. Investigate the right PID first and prefer a normal termination request. A real program can handle signals differently, and this exercise does not model supervisor restarts or graceful shutdown work.

concepts.title: Treat queue numbers as supplied facts
concepts.text: Recv-Q is fixed empty in this exercise’s snapshot. For TCP, Send-Q is the supplied limit for pending connections, often called backlog; for the unconnected UDP row it is zero. These are bounded teaching facts, not measured traffic or a guarantee of a working service. A paused owner may still have a LISTEN row, so preserve the approved owner’s process state as well as its endpoint.

concepts.title: Verify the state you meant to change
concepts.text: An ending command may finish without output. Inspect ss and ps afterward: the unwanted endpoint should disappear, while the local preview and approved service remain. This is current runtime state only; ending a process does not configure what starts at boot. Check work evaluates the resulting state, not whether you copied a particular command sequence.

practice.title: Relate an endpoint to its process
practice.action: Select ss -lntup, choose Insert command and then Run. Do the same for the worked ps command. Find TCP 0.0.0.0:9090 and compare its PID with the separate loopback instance.
practice.observe: The two sampled rows share a name but have different PIDs and endpoints. The UDP endpoint remains visible even though its foreign owner’s -p metadata is blank.

practice.title: Pause and re-inspect
practice.action: Insert and Run kill -STOP 6010, then ss -lntp. You can type ps -p 6010 -o pid,stat,comm and Run to inspect the paused state.
practice.observe: The process is paused, but its TCP 0.0.0.0:9090 row remains LISTEN. Paused is not closed, and the same-name loopback instance must not be changed.

practice.title: End only that example instance
practice.action: Insert and Run kill -CONT 6010, then kill -TERM 6010, then the final ss and ps commands. Read the new terminal output; it describes the actual current practice state.
practice.observe: The obsolete endpoint disappears. The loopback TCP, approved application TCP and UDP endpoints remain, and all unrelated processes keep their original state. The worked table is an expectation; these new command results are the actual observation.

worked.label: Find the intended example
worked.explanation: Compare protocol/address/port with the same-name loopback instance; a command name is not an instance identity.

worked.label: Expected after STOP
worked.explanation: The process changes phase but retains its bound endpoint. This is not successful retirement.

worked.label: Expected after CONT, then TERM
worked.explanation: The supplied active owner ends on the termination request; only that endpoint disappears.

worked.label: Expected protected work
worked.explanation: All three remain bound, and their unrelated owners keep their original process state. This does not prove real network reachability.

goal: Repair inherited search so the worker finds the right supplied tools while retaining its other settings.
context: Complete Keep a planning note in the parent and Locate the active application files first. You will reuse quoted assignments, export, absolute paths and file/directory permission bits; no host commands are needed.

concepts.title: A name needs somewhere to look
concepts.text: A command name such as labeltool does not identify its folder. PATH is a colon-separated list of directories. The worker tries them from left to right and selects the first eligible file with that name. Here the folders and files are supplied metadata in memory; selecting a file does not run it.

concepts.title: Make the current copy reachable first
concepts.text: In the gallery example, TOOL_DIR holds the current labeltool; LEGACY_DIR holds an older copy. BASE_PATH holds auditview and a labeltool file without execute permission. The worked setup puts TOOL_DIR before BASE_PATH. A disabled candidate is skipped; an earlier eligible old copy would win. The assignment uses reportgen and auditprobe in different folders.

concepts.title: Pass the search value to the worker
concepts.text: The worker gets the setup’s exported values. In export PATH="$TOOL_DIR:$BASE_PATH", the colon separates directories and the quotes keep the supplied text together. export marks the new value for inheritance. A newly assigned PATH is private unless exported; assigning to an already exported PATH keeps that attribute. A parent shell can use its own private PATH, but this task inspects a separate worker’s inherited value.

concepts.title: Permission to search is different from permission to list
concepts.text: A known path needs search permission (x) on every parent directory and execute permission (x) on the selected ordinary file. Read permission is not required for this metadata lookup. The supplied inventory is readonly; you repair the search value, not permissions. The allowed directory list means readonly for this modeled caller; it is not a general security guarantee.

concepts.title: Check the whole path and keep the report separate
concepts.text: Even an unused trailing directory must belong to the supplied readonly list. The lookup table shows which files the worker actually finds; it does not show utility output or prove the programs could start. A separate fixed child script reports TOKEN. Keep that report and every other supplied value unchanged while repairing PATH. Each run uses fresh sample inputs and reset simulated files.

concepts.title: A template is a starting copy
concepts.text: A skeleton directory is a set of starting files for a new home. In this exercise, useradd -m copies the saved /etc/skel; -k can choose another supplied skeleton. useradd -M makes only the account record. Existing homes are independent copies, not links to the template. A leading dot, as in .profile, marks a hidden filename; naming it explicitly lets you inspect it.

concepts.title: Save the standard before creating the account
concepts.text: The native Template file editor changes only the supplied known leaves. Edit File contents and the octal mode, then Save selected file. Clear Include in new homes for the removable draft note, then Remove selected file. Pending edits are not the saved template used by useradd. These are simulator editor controls, not Linux shell commands.

concepts.title: Text, permissions and ownership are separate
concepts.text: In the worked example, .profile needs mode 0640: its owner can read/write, its group can read and others have no access. welcome.txt needs 0644: owner read/write, group and others read. Copying retains these file modes but sets copied ownership to the new user’s UID and primary GID. Home mode 0700 is the supplied exercise policy, not a universal Linux default. These are file permission bits: home mode 0700 still prevents other users from traversing the home.

concepts.title: Create and verify both records and files
concepts.text: The annotated command below supplies every account value. The primary group must already exist. id maps memberships to numbers; ls -ld inspects each named file’s owner, group and mode; cat reads text. A correct account record alone does not prove that its home contains the repaired defaults. A copied .profile is only text here: no login or shell startup is being tested.

concepts.title: Changing a template is not a home update
concepts.text: After Lumi’s home exists, changing /etc/skel/.profile affects a later copy, not /home/lumi/.profile. Guided practice compares the two paths. Restore the worked template to finish the example. If you create your own trial account too early, repair its source first and carefully remove/recreate only that trial account and home; never remove existing users to repair their defaults.

goal: Repair why the preferred report command is skipped, keeping the audit tool and fallback intact.
context: Build on file paths, owner/group/other permissions and ordered PATH. Type in the input below the terminal transcript; Run or Enter submits one simulated command. This practice uses different names and folders from the assignment.

concepts.title: A name is searched in order
concepts.text: PATH is an ordered list of folders, separated by colons. A command name can exist in several folders. which NAME prints the first eligible executable file; type -a -p NAME lists all eligible external files in PATH order. The printed paths are search results, not a command run.

concepts.title: Present is different from executable
concepts.text: A regular file can exist and be readable yet lack permission to execute. Search skips that file and may select a later copy. ls -l PATH shows its permission letters and owner. In -rw-r----- the owner has read/write, the group has read and nobody has execute. The x letter means execute for a file; on folders it means permission to search through them.

concepts.title: Repair only what the task permits
concepts.text: Alex owns the preferred file. chmod u+x PATH adds execute for its owner while preserving every other permission bit. u means owner, + means add and x means execute. chmod u-x removes only that bit. A silent chmod is normal; inspect the file and repeat lookup to verify the change. Do not grant permissions to everyone or disable the fallback.

concepts.title: Inspect without running a file
concepts.text: These supplied command files contain sample text. The simulated terminal supports which, type -a -p, ls and chmod for this activity; it does not run a found path or any file contents. The supplied PATH is fixed. Aliases, shell functions, command hashing, plain type and whereis are outside this activity.

concepts.title: A fast search can use yesterday’s names
concepts.text: find walks the supplied virtual folders now. locate searches a separate saved list of names. A deleted or renamed file can still appear in that list, and a new file can be missing. Reading a returned path with cat checks the file’s actual contents.

concepts.title: Exclusions affect the next rebuild
concepts.text: The native editor changes the PRUNEPATHS setting: quoted absolute folders whose contents should be skipped. A folder’s own name may remain listed; its descendants are excluded. An exact archive exclusion does not hide the separate archives folder. Save configuration applies the text; it does not update the saved list. Real system defaults commonly use /etc/updatedb.conf. Here you edit the supplied private file, so this exercise affects only its private index.

concepts.title: Rebuild explicitly, then verify
concepts.text: updatedb -l 0 -o DATABASE -U ROOT --config-file CONFIG builds this activity’s private index. Each path is supplied by the lesson. A successful rebuild prints nothing. locate -e -d DATABASE TEXT filters saved names by current existence; it does not add missing names or refresh the index.

concepts.title: A filename is not proof of the right document
concepts.text: Use cat PATH to read a file and cp SOURCE DEST to copy it. Read the current and archive files before copying. The assignment checks the saved exclusions, a fresh index and the actual handover contents, while preserving everything else. All commands and files stay inside the simulator; this private-index exercise does not reproduce system-wide access or visibility rules.

goal: Add restricted deletion without locking teammates out or claiming that it protects writable file contents.
context: After ordinary owner/group access and safe file handovers. Work as the supplied simulated participant; no real accounts or setup are needed.

concepts.title: A folder controls its names
concepts.text: Read permission lets someone list names. Write plus search permission lets them add or remove names. A file’s own read/write bits control its contents, so making a file read-only does not by itself protect its name from removal.

concepts.title: Add one ownership rule
concepts.text: The sticky flag, also called restricted deletion, keeps normal directory permissions and adds a removal rule. An ordinary participant must own the entry or own its containing directory to remove or replace its name. The participant still needs normal write and search permission.

concepts.title: Read t and T correctly
concepts.text: In ls -ld, t means sticky and other-user search are both set. T means sticky is set but other-user search is absent. Both enable restricted deletion. It does not stop writing into an existing file when that file’s own permissions allow the write.

concepts.title: A move can replace two names
concepts.text: Moving a file removes its old name. If the destination already exists, the move also replaces that name. Each sticky containing directory checks the entry’s owner separately.

concepts.title: An unused name avoids a replacement
concepts.text: Taylor owns the practice draft, while Morgan owns the existing release. Publishing to the supplied new Taylor name needs directory write and search but does not replace Morgan’s entry. The sticky policy stays intact.

concepts.title: Writing data is a different operation
concepts.text: Copying into an existing writable file changes its contents without removing its name. Sticky does not block that write. Preserve the colleague’s data; do not treat the flag as a complete file-security solution.

concepts.title: Separate the device from its driver
concepts.text: The kernel is the core of Linux that manages hardware. A device is the supplied controller; its driver is code that lets the kernel work with it. In this simulation the controller needs a loadable module. lspci -k distinguishes a possible module from a driver currently in use. Real Linux also has built-in drivers, which this exercise does not model.

concepts.title: Read dependencies before loading
concepts.text: A dependency is another module that must be loaded first. lsmod lists loaded modules. modinfo shows the supplied module object and its hard dependencies. insmod inserts one object and requires those dependencies already loaded; modprobe uses the current lookup index to load them in order. Use the module name with modprobe, an exact supplied object path with insmod.

concepts.title: Verify and preserve other providers

concepts.title: A table entry is not a filesystem
concepts.text: An MBR describes regions of a disk. Its main table has four slots. A primary partition uses one slot directly; its Linux data or swap hint describes intended use, but does not create those contents. This task uses two primary payloads.

concepts.title: Read both ends of a range
concepts.text: Ranges include Start and End. With 512-byte sectors, capacity is (End − Start + 1) × 512. In the worked example, sectors 4096–12287 contain 8192 sectors: 4 MiB. An aligned start is a multiple of the supplied 2048-sector alignment.

concepts.title: Free space is not another primary slot

concepts.title: Put logical payloads inside one container
concepts.text: An extended container describes a region; do not format it. Logical payloads inside it start at partition number 5 and have their own ranges and contents. A logical payload cannot extend beyond its container or overlap another payload.

concepts.title: Leave space for layout metadata
concepts.text: This exercise reserves one explicit sector for each logical payload before its data, inside the container. Current reservations are shown under the table. This is a disclosed EBR teaching model, not raw chains or actual parted placement. The worked aligned starts leave room for metadata; simply packing all data sectors together can fail.

goal: Inspect aging metadata, set a rotation deadline and warn before it, without inventing a password change.
context: After local account and group administration.

concepts.title: Read the record before changing policy
concepts.text: Aging records store when a password was last changed and the policy around that date. chage -l ACCOUNT lists those fields. It does not check a password or prove that someone can log in. Here the records and dates are supplied samples; there is no actual password to enter.

concepts.title: Maximum age is counted from the last change
concepts.text: The maximum is a number of UTC days after the recorded last change. In this versioned policy model, taylor last changed on 2027-03-10 and a 20 day maximum reaches its deadline on 2027-03-30. On that date the policy requires a password change. Changing the record is not an actual password change.

concepts.title: A warning gives notice; it does not extend the deadline
concepts.text: A 4 day warning begins on 2027-03-26: four days remain until March 30. -M (capital M) sets maximum days; -W sets warning days. Keep the last-change history intact instead of making it look newer.

concepts.title: Recognize the fields you must preserve
concepts.text: Minimum days restrict how soon a password may be changed again; they do not deny ordinary use. Inactivity is a grace counted after password expiry, not time since the last login. Account expiry is a separate fixed date. This task changes only maximum and warning.

concepts.title: Apply one command, then compare dates
concepts.text: A command has a utility name, options with values, and the account name: chage -M 20 -W 4 taylor. Run command changes the virtual record. Check aging policy compares fields, protected accounts and each supplied date. Other supported option spellings can reach the same state.

worked.label: Inspect practice metadata
worked.explanation: Read the last-change date and existing maximum/warning before changing anything.

worked.label: Set the two requested fields
worked.explanation: Changes only maximum and warning. The last-change date remains 2027-03-10.

worked.label: Connect the dates
worked.value:
March 10 +20 days = March 30
March 30 −4 days = March 26
worked.explanation: Warning begins March 26; password change is required at March 30. The separate 5 day grace ends April 4 in this model.

practice.action: Choose Insert record query, then Run command. Read the last-change date, maximum and warning in the terminal.
practice.observe: The command field is editable; inserting a query does not execute it.

practice.action: Type chage -M 20 -W 4 taylor, then Run command and Check aging policy. Compare the March 26 and March 30 rows.
practice.observe: Expected and Actual are separate: the warning appears before the password-change requirement. A passing row is a matching policy observation, not successful authentication.

practice.action: Run chage -W 0 taylor and Check aging policy again. Read the warning feedback, then restore 4 days and retry. Optional worked commands insert text only.
practice.observe: The deadline stays the same, but advance warning disappears. Your separate assignment remains untouched.

goal: Distinguish a required password change from an ended grace period, then repair only the grace.
context: Builds on the preceding password-aging assignment; review its Introduction if needed.

concepts.title: Expired does not mean the password became valid again
concepts.text: At maximum age this model requires a password change. A grace period leaves that requirement in place; it does not grant unrestricted login or perform a password change. When grace ends, administrative recovery is needed under this modeled policy.

concepts.title: Inactivity begins after password expiry
concepts.text: Despite its name, this field is not a timer since the last login. Add maximum age to the recorded last change to find password expiry; add inactivity days to find the end of grace. A zero grace ends immediately at expiry. Disabled grace (-1) is different from zero.

concepts.title: Change the grace field without rewriting history
concepts.text: chage -I 4 lee sets four days of inactivity grace. -I is a capital i; it is different from lowercase -i, which asks for ISO date output on a list query. Keep -M, -W and -d untouched in this repair.

concepts.title: Test both sides of the boundary
concepts.text: For practice, August 10 plus 14 days is August 24. A 4 day grace runs until August 28; on August 27 a password change is still required, and on August 28 grace has ended. The table models one pinned policy, not all distribution login stacks.

goal: Combine a finite account-date handover with a preserved password-reset requirement and protected records.
context: Builds on the preceding password-aging assignment; review its Introduction if needed.

concepts.title: A fixed account date is a separate limit
concepts.text: Account expiry is a fixed UTC date, regardless of how old a password is. In this model it is checked first. An expired contract date can therefore hide a still-pending password-reset requirement.

concepts.title: A reset marker is not a recorded date
concepts.text: A last-change value of 0 means a password change is required; it is not a claim that the password changed on January 1,1970. chage -l displays password must be changed. Keep this intentional marker during the handover; there is no password-change operation in this activity.

concepts.title: Extend the account without clearing the reset
concepts.text: chage -E 2027-02-22 casey changes only the fixed account date. The -E value may be a supported YYYY-MM-DD date or positive epoch-day number. -E -1 would remove the date entirely; that is not a finite extension. Changing -d would alter the reset/history field.

Request an initially read-only root and ordinary multi-user startup. Test the edited entry until all requested outcomes match.

concepts.title: A boot entry describes the next attempt, not the running computer
concepts.text: Firmware first makes a boot loader available. This activity starts after that handoff: the loader can read a supplied boot partition, written as $BOOT. A small Type #1 .conf file points to a kernel and optional early-boot images. Test entry predicts the supplied path; it neither reboots nor changes a real system.

concepts.title: Read a Type #1 entry as key and literal value
concepts.text: Each line starts with a key, a space and its value. linux names a kernel image; initrd names an initial RAM filesystem image. These paths start at the root of the same virtual boot partition, not at your running Linux root. title and version describe a menu item; changing them does not change which image loads. Lines beginning with # are comments. This is configuration text, not a shell script. Several options lines add kernel arguments in order; they form one combined command line.

concepts.title: The kernel and early userspace must reach the real root
concepts.text: The kernel initializes basic hardware. An initramfs provides a temporary early userspace and matching loadable drivers before the real system root is available. Here it also resolves root=UUID= to the supplied filesystem identifier. A UUID identifies a filesystem independently of its menu title. The storage and filesystem drivers must be built in or available from matching early-boot images before that filesystem can be mounted.

concepts.title: Reaching a filesystem is not the same as starting the intended system
concepts.text: The real root must contain a working init program. These supplied systems use systemd: systemd.unit=rescue.target requests recovery after the modeled handoff, while multi-user.target requests ordinary text-mode startup. ro requests an initially read-only root; later remounting and actual services are outside this activity. The trace distinguishes a missing image, blocked early userspace, an inaccessible root and a missing init program.

concepts.title: Apply the evidence in this lesson
concepts.text: The entry loads its kernel and initramfs, but the archive has no init program. The right repair changes the root=UUID= argument using the filesystem inventory; a different title cannot redirect the handoff.

goal: Diagnose a failed upgrade and select the supplied ordinary fallback without damaging another boot path.
requirements: Select the supplied known-working 7.0 ordinary entry for system UUID 31415926-5358-9793-2384-626433832795; use an explicit default.
Preserve all three supplied entries’ titles, image paths and kernel settings. A recovery target or repaired 7.1 upgrade is not the requested fallback.

concepts.title: A menu chooses one complete boot entry
concepts.text: The earlier boot-entry lessons described one kernel handoff. A GRUB menu can hold several entries: each has a readable title, a short identifier written as --id=..., and commands between { and }. set default chooses which entry will be tried. This lesson supplies GRUB’s readable boot partition; it does not install a loader or boot a computer.

concepts.title: Read the choice, then the image commands
concepts.text: A default can name an existing ID, a quoted title, or a zero-based position: 0 means the first entry and 1 the second. An ID still selects the same entry if its position changes. linux names the kernel and its arguments; initrd follows it and supplies the early userspace. Selecting a different title does not repair the files inside that entry.

concepts.title: Keep two meanings of root separate
concepts.text: GRUB first needs a filesystem from which to read its files. That file-reading root is supplied here, and paths such as /workshop/7.0/linux start there. Linux then uses root=UUID= on its kernel command line to find the intended system filesystem. That UUID is not a menu title or a substitute for the kernel path.

concepts.title: Read and edit a small menu
concepts.text: GRUB has its own configuration language. Quotes keep a title containing spaces together; # starts a comment at a word boundary. A backslash at a physical line’s end joins the next line, so long kernel arguments can remain readable. Close each entry with } on its own line. Write values directly: expressions and other kinds of GRUB script are outside this activity.

concepts.title: Test the requested result, preserve the other path
concepts.text: Test menu shows which entry was selected and traces kernel, early userspace, system root and init handoff. A bootable entry can still use the wrong release or target for your task. In this model ro is the initial root mode; systemd.unit=rescue.target requests recovery, while multi-user.target requests ordinary startup. Later remounts and actual services are outside this activity.

requirements: Generate a menu that selects the supplied 7.0 ordinary-startup entry for system UUID 31415926-5358-9793-2384-626433832795.

concepts.title: Settings describe the next generated menu
concepts.text: /etc/default/grub stores source settings. A generated grub.cfg-style menu is a separate result. In this activity, type in Persistent boot settings, choose Generate menu · simulation, then Test generated menu · simulation. Editing alone leaves the previous generated menu outdated. On Linux, grub-mkconfig generates configuration from settings and scripts. Here Generate menu models only the supplied-template portion; that program is never run.

concepts.title: Choose an entry and allow time to choose another
concepts.text: GRUB_DEFAULT can name a supplied entry ID, its quoted title, or its position counted from zero. GRUB_TIMEOUT is the wait in seconds: 0 starts immediately, -1 waits for a selection. This simulator allows -1 or 0–300. IDs survive order changes more clearly than numeric positions.

concepts.title: Normal-only does not mean whichever entry is selected
concepts.text: The supplied templates identify normal and recovery entries. GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX adds arguments to every Linux entry. GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT adds more arguments only to normal entries, after the common ones, regardless of GRUB_DEFAULT. Keep quiet off recovery when diagnostic messages are needed.

context: Use the previous GRUB menu and early-boot lessons for entry IDs, image paths, UUIDs and recovery targets. This lesson introduces source settings and generation before you use them. Literal NAME=value settings have no spaces around =; quote a value containing spaces, and use # for a comment after whitespace.

concepts.text: The supplied templates already include the system root and initial ro. GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX is appended to both normal and recovery entries; GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT follows it only on normal entries. In this model, a later rw overrides an earlier ro. Inspect the generated arguments before diagnosing the image files.

concepts.title: Keep diagnostics available on recovery
concepts.text: quiet requests fewer kernel messages. A quiet in the common setting reaches recovery too. Put normal-only options in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT; its DEFAULT suffix refers to the normal template class, not the selected GRUB_DEFAULT entry. An empty quoted value adds no arguments.

concepts.title: Verify the generated result after every edit
concepts.text: Persistent settings, generated menu and tested results are separate. A valid selected entry alone cannot prove the recovery path or its arguments are correct. Generate after editing and read every entry requirement in Actual test result. Old generated output remains visible as outdated until you regenerate.

context: Use the previous GRUB menu and early-boot lessons for entry IDs, image paths, UUIDs and recovery targets. This lesson introduces source settings and generation before you use them. Literal NAME=value settings have no spaces around =; quote a value containing spaces, and use # for a comment after whitespace.

worked.value:
normal: template options + GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX + GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT
recovery: template options + GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX
worked.explanation: Common options affect both classes. The worked settings add quiet only to normal entries and leave each template’s root, image paths and initial ro intact.

Settings edited → generated menu OUTDATED
Generate menu → current read-only menu
Test generated menu → entry traces and task outcomes

goal: Recover a BIOS startup path by distinguishing the installation disk from the mounted boot directory.
requirements: Repair the GRUB BIOS installation on the supplied startup disk /dev/vda using the existing configured boot directory.
Reach the Operations system UUID 12345678-9abc-def0-1234-56789abcdef0 with kernel 7.0, initially read-only, and ordinary multi-user startup.
Preserve every partition and filesystem, and the archive loader on /dev/vdb. Test the current boot chain after your final repair.
context: Complete the MBR layout and GRUB configuration units first. A whole disk such as /dev/vdc contains partitions such as /dev/vdc1. Here a supplied rescue environment already has the target filesystem mounted; you do not prepare a VM, mount your own disk or run commands outside this app.

concepts.title: Follow the boot chain
concepts.text: BIOS selects a disk. The MBR’s boot code starts GRUB’s core in the free sectors before the first partition. GRUB then reads its files and menu from the boot directory. The menu selects the kernel, initramfs and root filesystem studied in the earlier lessons.

concepts.title: Keep disk and directory separate
concepts.text: grub-install DISK installs boot code for that whole device. --boot-directory=PATH chooses where GRUB’s files live. The command’s default /boot belongs to this rescue environment, which may differ from the mounted target. Inspect the supplied directories before choosing; a successful command on the wrong disk does not repair the selected startup disk.

concepts.title: Install, then verify
concepts.text: The supplied i386-pc package models GRUB for BIOS. Its 512-sector core must fit the actual gap after sector 0 and before the first partition. Here the first partition starts at sector 2048, so 2047 sectors are available. Installation does not create grub.cfg. Test boot chain follows the installed disk, directory, menu and images; it also checks the preserved archive loader.

worked.label: Inspect the separate workshop
worked.explanation: Read each command separately in the console. The supplied BIOS starts at /dev/vdc; /workshop/boot contains its intended system menu. /boot is a different, empty rescue location.

worked.label: Install to the intended whole disk
worked.explanation: The destination is /dev/vdc, not /dev/vdc1. --boot-directory names the mounted directory containing the supplied menu. The archive loader on /dev/vdd must stay untouched.

worked.label: Verify the resulting state
worked.value: Run command → Test boot chain · simulation
worked.explanation: The native Test button is a simulator action. Read the actual stages and task outcomes. Changing the installed path clears its previous test; inventory-only commands do not change installed state.

practice.title: Inspect before installing
practice.action: Type lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS and choose Run command. Compare the startup disk and mounted directories in Supplied machine. Use findmnt -T /workshop/boot and cat /workshop/boot/grub/grub.cfg to investigate.
practice.observe: Actual console output comes from these supplied facts. The target menu exists in /workshop/boot; rescue /boot has none.

practice.title: Repair and test the workshop
practice.action: Enter the workshop installation command from the Introduction, or open Worked practice and choose Insert command. Choose Run command, then Test boot chain · simulation.
practice.observe: The actual boot test should reach Practice outcomes match, including the preserved /dev/vdd loader. Insertion alone does not run a command.

practice.action: Run grub-install /dev/vdc, then Test boot chain. Read the blocked menu stage, restore the configured boot directory and test again.
practice.observe: The command can install successfully while boot testing fails: its default /boot has no menu. The feedback explains that installation does not generate one.

goal: Recover UEFI startup by installing a loader on the intended EFI partition and registering its firmware path.
requirements: Restore the Operations boot path through the EFI System Partition on /dev/vda1.
Use the supplied kernel 7.0 and root UUID 7240d4ce-f757-4103-be48-d903f6e7e9c9 with initially read-only root and ordinary multi-user startup.
Preserve Boot0007 and every file on the archive EFI partition. Keep the archive after the intended working entry in BootOrder.
Test the current boot chain after your final installation or firmware change.
context: Start after the BIOS recovery and GPT disk preparation lessons. This rescue environment already supplies the mounted filesystems. The EFI System Partition, or ESP, holds the EFI executable. The ordinary boot directory holds the GRUB menu and Linux boot files.

concepts.title: Find the EFI System Partition
concepts.text: The supplied GPT partition role identifies an ESP and FAT32 stores its files. The GPT partition GUID identifies the partition to firmware. The FAT volume serial describes its filesystem. The ext4 root UUID identifies the Linux system to its kernel. Read the disk, partition number and Linux mount together.

concepts.title: Install the file into the right mounted filesystem
concepts.text: On the supplied x86_64-efi system, --efi-directory points to the mounted ESP. --boot-directory points to the directory with the configured GRUB menu. These directories can reside on different disks. Firmware stores boot entries in memory called NVRAM. With --no-nvram, installation leaves those entries and BootOrder untouched.

concepts.title: Register and check the actual boot path
concepts.text: An efibootmgr entry identifies the disk, partition and EFI path. Use backslashes in the firmware path and single quotes to preserve them. The path starts inside the ESP, independent of its Linux mount. BootOrder lists hexadecimal entry numbers. Firmware tries active entries in order and can skip a missing executable. A later Linux handoff failure needs repair after the application starts.

worked.label: Inspect the workshop before repair
worked.explanation: Run one command at a time. The workshop ESP is /dev/vdc1 at /workshop/esp. The boot directory with the supplied menu is /workshop/boot. Boot0009 initially starts the archive.

worked.label: Install the workshop application
worked.explanation: Enter this as one command, including --no-nvram. The file appears on the EFI partition. BootOrder still starts Boot0009 until you register the new file.

worked.label: Register the partition-relative path
worked.explanation: The disk and partition refer to /dev/vdc1. The single quotes preserve the backslashes. Creating an option adds it to the front of BootOrder while retaining Boot0009. Use Test boot chain to verify the resulting startup.

practice.title: Identify the two locations
practice.action: Run lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS and efibootmgr -v. Compare the workshop ESP mount with its configured boot directory.
practice.observe: Actual console output shows the FAT32 partition and archive boot entry. The mounted ext4 boot directory is separate.

practice.title: Install and inspect the partial repair
practice.action: Enter the workshop installation command from the Introduction or insert it from Worked practice. Run it, then choose Test boot chain · simulation.
practice.observe: The new EFI file is present. The archive still starts because the installation left BootOrder unchanged.

practice.title: Register and test the loader
practice.action: Choose Test boot chain if you have just installed the file. Then run the workshop efibootmgr create command. Read the new entry and order in actual output, and test again.
practice.observe: With only the file installed, the archive still starts. After registration the intended workshop entry starts before the preserved archive.

practice.title: Observe the effect of order
practice.action: Put the archive first with efibootmgr -o and the two actual numbers. Test, restore the working order, and test again.
practice.observe: A new order clears the prior result. The test tells you which application starts.

concepts.title: A reply does not guarantee a usable clock
concepts.text: Chrony can receive responses without having enough good samples to use a server. In chronyc sources, the first symbol ^ means server. A second symbol ? means it cannot be selected in this observation. A star marks the selected source.

concepts.title: Read the last eight polls
concepts.text: Reach records whether recent polls got valid responses. The octal value 377 means eight replies, and 0 means no replies in the last eight polls. This field reports reachability. It does not decide whether the clock can use a source.

concepts.text: Each server line names one supplied IPv4 address. Optional iburst requests quicker initial sampling in real chrony. Here the sample observations are already supplied. Apply configuration changes the list used by the simulated client. The local time zone is a display setting and stays unchanged.

requirements: Open the supplied journal copy at /recovery/field-journal and list its boots.

context: Build on terminal command entry and the Linux facility/priority introduction. No rescue-system setup is needed.

concepts.title: Open the copy from the affected machine
concepts.text: A rescue environment has its own logs. Use -D with the supplied copied journal directory to read the affected system’s records.

concepts.title: Identify one boot from the time window
concepts.text: A boot ID is a 32-character identifier. List the copied boots and compare the incident time to the first and last entry for each boot. Use the full ID with -b.

concepts.title: Filter the evidence
concepts.text: Use -u for the service and -p for the urgency threshold. Smaller numbers are more urgent, so warning (4) includes errors (3) and more urgent levels. Use -o cat to show only the message text.

worked.label: List boots in the copied journal

practice.observe: Find the boot whose first and last entries surround 09:17 UTC.

concepts.title: A mail client hands messages to a mail transfer agent
concepts.text: A mail transfer agent, or MTA, routes messages toward recipients. Postfix, Sendmail and Exim are common examples. Here, sample messages stay among the supplied simulated local users.

concepts.title: An alias is a shared recipient name
concepts.text: An aliases entry has a name before a colon and comma-separated recipients after it. Mail sent to that name expands to those recipients. Aliases can point through other aliases.

concepts.title: The saved text and lookup are separate
concepts.text: Editing /etc/aliases changes its source text. Rebuild aliases represents the newaliases command that refreshes the lookup used for delivery. Test both the team route and the protected administrative route.

concepts.title: A forwarding file belongs to one recipient
concepts.text: A user's .forward file lists where that user's incoming mail should go. Write only its recipient list, without an alias name or colon. Save this file before sending a test message.

concepts.text: A .forward file containing only another user's name sends the message to that user. Including the file owner's own name keeps a copy in the owner's mailbox as well. An empty file keeps ordinary local delivery.

concepts.title: Forwarding is read when mail is delivered
concepts.text: The saved .forward file takes effect on the next delivery. Rebuild aliases updates the separate aliases lookup. Keep other mail routes working.

goal: Place a log filesystem where its future growth space is actually adjacent.
context: Review the disk-preparation unit: read supplied media, count inclusive sectors, distinguish hints from initialized content and preserve existing data. Now plan where partitions go in relation to one another.

concepts.title: Plan for the growing data
concepts.text: Logs record activity and often grow. A preserved archive can divide a disk into several free intervals. Choose a region that holds today’s log partition and leaves the requested space immediately after it.

concepts.title: Adjacent space is different from total space
concepts.text: A raw partition occupies consecutive sectors. To extend its end in place later, the following sectors must be unallocated. A large free interval elsewhere does not remove the next partition blocking its end. This lesson reserves room; it does not perform a resize.

concepts.title: Read the units and count both ends
concepts.text: These virtual disks use 512-byte sectors. One MiB is 1,048,576 bytes, so one MiB contains 2048 sectors. For a chosen size, end = start + size in sectors − 1. The − 1 matters because both endpoints belong to the partition. Starts must be multiples of the supplied 2048-sector alignment.

concepts.title: Keep the growth window unallocated
concepts.text: Do not create a “reserve” partition in the growth window. Even an unformatted partition occupies its sectors. The model counts only unused sectors between your log partition and the next allocation or the GPT metadata at the disk’s end.

concepts.title: Allocate, then initialize content
concepts.text: A Linux data hint describes intended use. It does not create an ext4 filesystem. After adding the partition, select its actual number and initialize ext4 with the required label. Keep the supplied archive and its file intact.

concepts.title: Explore safely in the separate example
concepts.text: Fill selected step changes draft fields only. Add and Initialize change the virtual disk; Check current disk configuration evaluates it. This preparation model cannot delete, resize or overwrite allocations. If an experiment consumes needed space, Reset practice and replay the example. The small MiB capacities are examples for calculating space, not real-system sizing advice.

requirements: On /dev/vda create exactly one aligned partition named logs, 8–12 MiB inclusive, with a Linux data hint and actual ext4 label logs.
Leave at least 16 MiB of unallocated sectors immediately after logs, before the next partition or reserved GPT tail.
Preserve the archive partition and /keep.txt, the existing GPT and all unrequested allocations.
No mounting or resizing is required.

practice.title: Read the layout before allocating

practice.action: Use Add partition using draft for each intended extent, inspect its actual number, then Initialize selected blank partition with the requested format/label. Select Check current disk configuration.
practice.observe: A role can have the correct size but still fail because its signature, following free space or disk relationship is wrong.

practice.title: Consume a growth window, then recover
practice.action: After success, add scratch on /dev/vde at sectors 79872–81919 inclusive using a Linux data hint. Check again. Use Reset practice and replay to recover.

goal: Allocate root, logs and swap while preserving startup data and independent growth pools.
context: Review the disk-preparation unit: read supplied media, count inclusive sectors, distinguish hints from initialized content and preserve existing data. Now plan where partitions go in relation to one another.

concepts.title: Choose a role for each future filesystem
concepts.text: The root filesystem / holds the main directory tree; /var holds changing data such as logs, and /home holds users’ files. /boot holds startup files. Swap is paging space rather than an ordinary filesystem. Names here record intended roles; mounting, swap activation and bootloader installation are separate tasks.

concepts.title: Two partitions are not two disks
concepts.text: Separate fixed filesystems already isolate their ordinary file allocations, even on one disk. This team additionally requires root and logs on different supplied disks so their replacement and future unallocated growth pools can be managed independently. This is a placement policy, not a measurement of I/O performance or hardware failure domains.

concepts.title: Leave a useful growth window
concepts.text: A log partition needs the stated unused space immediately after its end. Put another role somewhere else if it would consume that window. Count inclusive sectors and the reserved GPT tail, rather than treating the entire disk as usable.

concepts.title: Preserve the supplied startup reference
concepts.text: The existing boot-ref partition and /keep.txt are provided data. Keep their location, content and identity unchanged. Only the other supplied disk needs a new GPT. These reference files do not establish that a real operating system would boot.

concepts.title: Check actual signatures and labels
concepts.text: Root and logs need actual ext4 content; swap needs an actual swap signature. Partition hints, names and draft fields alone are incomplete. Any valid unique UUID and any placement/order meeting the required sizes, alignment, disk separation and growth window can work.

concepts.title: Plan before applying an allocation
concepts.text: Add commits a virtual allocation, and this bounded preparation model has no delete or resize. In the separate example, a scratch partition demonstrates a bad growth window; Reset practice and replay to recover. The independent assignment remains your own draft and applied state.

requirements: Preserve /dev/vda1 boot-ref and its /keep.txt, including its extent, content and identity.

On /dev/vda or /dev/vdb create exactly one aligned root partition of 16–24 MiB with actual ext4 label root, one logs partition of 12–20 MiB with actual ext4 label logs, and one swap partition of 4–8 MiB with actual swap label swap.
Use Linux data hints for root and logs, and a Linux swap hint for swap.
Place root and logs on different supplied disks, and leave at least 24 MiB unallocated immediately after logs.
Create GPT only on the eligible blank disk and keep all unrequested allocations unchanged; mounting, activation and boot installation are not required.

practice.observe: A role can have the correct size but still fail because its signature, following free space or disk relationship is wrong.

practice.title: Consume a growth window, then recover
practice.action: After success, add scratch on /dev/vdf at sectors 20480–22527 inclusive using a Linux data hint. Check again. Use Reset practice and replay to recover.
practice.observe: The log filesystem can remain correctly formatted while adjacent growth space and preservation fail. This model does not delete or undo an allocation.

goal: Distinguish accepting new requests from starting a printer, then deliver the requested copies of a supplied document.
context: Builds on the file/terminal foundations. All documents and printers are supplied; the commands operate only on this in-memory activity.
requirements: Make office accept new requests and process pending jobs; keep it as your local default.
Deliver exactly two new copies of /work/agenda.txt to office. Sample checks alone do not submit your assignment.
Preserve labels settings and its held request labels-41. Leave no extra unfinished requests or unintended completed documents.

practice.title: Inspect and admit new work
practice.action: Run lpstat -t. Find study and compare its accepting and enabled states. Run cupsaccept study; inspect again with lpstat -a study.
practice.observe: Accepting can change while the printer remains stopped. The protected label queue must stay as supplied.

practice.title: Submit, observe waiting, then start processing
practice.action: Run lpr -P study -# 2 workshop-note.txt, then lpq -l -P study. Start it with cupsenable study; run lpstat -W completed -o study.
practice.observe: lpr has no ordinary success message. The request first waits, then completes when the printer is enabled. Long lpq output shows requested copies.

practice.title: Check and diagnose a deliberate regression
practice.action: Choose Check example work. Run cupsdisable study, then check again. Repair it with cupsenable study and recheck; do not submit another two copies.
practice.observe: The original copies remain completed, but future requests now wait. Overall success clears when the printer is stopped.

concepts.title: A printer and its waiting line
concepts.text: A print queue holds requests for a printer. Accepting controls whether new requests may join that line. Enabled controls whether the printer processes waiting work. A queue can accept work while its printer is stopped; starting a printer does not necessarily reopen a queue that rejects new work.

concepts.title: Read both controls before changing them
concepts.text: Type a command in the simulated terminal and choose Run command, or press Return. lpstat -t summarizes printers, accepting states, default destination and active requests. lpstat -a focuses on accepting; lpstat -p focuses on processing. Files are supplied under /work; ls and cat let you inspect them.

concepts.title: Submit copies, then inspect the actual request
concepts.text: lp -d PRINTER -n COPIES FILE submits a document. The BSD-compatible form is lpr -P PRINTER -# COPIES FILE; -# is one option word, not a comment. Both use the same modeled queues. lp reports a request ID; lpr is normally silent, so inspect its request with lpq -P PRINTER. Neither a successful submission nor a queued request proves the document printed.

concepts.title: Verify completed work and the next request
concepts.text: cupsenable starts processing; cupsaccept allows new requests. Pending means waiting, Held means individually paused, and Completed means delivered in this finite simulator. lpstat -W completed -o PRINTER shows retained finished requests; -W goes before -o. Check print work evaluates actual deliveries and separate sample requests without adding jobs to your assignment. No real printer or CUPS service is used.

practice.observe: demo-reports is ready, but this one request remains held. The numeric Job value in lpq refers to the same request.

practice.title: Compare starting a printer with releasing a job
practice.action: Run cupsenable demo-reports, then inspect the request again. Now run lp -i demo-reports-27 -H resume and lpstat -W completed -o demo-reports.
practice.observe: The first command does not release the hold. The second finishes the original request with its existing document and copy count.

practice.action: Choose Check example work. Run lpr -q -P demo-reports demo-report.txt, inspect its new numeric Job value with lpq, and use lprm NUMBER to cancel only that new experiment; replace NUMBER with its actual Job value. Check again.
practice.observe: An extra held request prevents a clean handover. Withdrawing the new request repairs that mistake; the original completed request and protected label job remain.

concepts.title: A job can be paused while its printer is ready
concepts.text: A printer-level stop affects processing for that printer. An individual Held request is paused separately. Enabling an already ready printer will not release that hold. Inspect lpstat -l -o PRINTER to distinguish a held request from an ordinary pending one.

concepts.title: Identify the existing request
concepts.text: lpstat uses complete identifiers such as PRINTER-27. lpq shows the same request as a numeric Job value. Those are two views of one request, not two different queues. lpq -l also shows the document and copy count. Use the actual ID from the supplied state.

concepts.title: Resume the request instead of printing a replacement
concepts.text: lp -i REQUEST -H resume releases that request to its existing printer. If the printer is ready it completes in this model; if the printer is stopped it becomes pending. Reprinting the file creates a new request and does not finish the original held one.

concepts.title: Withdraw an unfinished mistake carefully
concepts.text: cancel REQUEST or lprm NUMBER ends an unfinished request. Cancellation is different from releasing a hold. Use the numeric Job value for lprm in this subset; implicit current-job and cancel-all forms are unsupported. An already completed wrong print cannot be erased by cancellation. Preserve the unrelated label request.

practice.action: Run lpstat -t and lpstat -l -o spare-labels; use lpq -l -P spare-labels to compare documents. Find the wrong default and misplaced request spare-labels-29. Do not start the label printer.
practice.observe: The default points new work at the wrong queue, and an earlier pending request already lives there. The legitimate label request is separately held.

concepts.title: A default affects new requests, not existing ones
concepts.text: A submission without -d or -P uses the local default in this activity. lpstat -d shows it; lpoptions -d PRINTER changes it. Changing the default does not move an existing request already waiting on another printer. The simulator does not model environment-variable or server-default precedence.

concepts.title: Investigate before starting every printer
concepts.text: lpstat -t and lpstat -l -o PRINTER expose queue controls, destination and request IDs. lpq -l -P PRINTER identifies the requested document and copies. A wrong pending request might print if you blindly enable its printer. Compare the requested document with the protected label work before changing anything.

concepts.title: Repair each layer deliberately
concepts.text: Withdraw the misplaced unfinished request using cancel REQUEST or lprm NUMBER. Reopen and enable only the intended printer, select the intended local default, then submit the required new copies. Leave the other printer and its legitimate held request alone.

concepts.title: Verify actual delivery and independent future behavior
concepts.text: A correct explicit-destination print can hide a wrong default. Conversely, a correct default does not fix an earlier misplaced job. Check print work evaluates current configuration, preserved request identity, actual completed copies and several separate sample requests. The sample jobs do not change your assignment.

context: Builds on file and terminal foundations. All files, settings and execution are supplied by this simulator.
requirements: Make current and fresh-login warehouse sample reports use German headings, preserve complete UTF-8 item names and use a decimal point for amounts.
Repair saved locale defaults as well as the current process; changing only one is insufficient. Save the settings editor before checking.
Verify both supplied report inputs. Inputs and all work are simulated; do not change host locale settings.

practice.title: Inspect a real sample result and its process settings
practice.action: Select /work/demo-morning.csv, choose Run sample report, then run locale and locale -k decimal_point in the simulated terminal. Compare LC_ALL with LANG and LC_NUMERIC.
practice.observe: The example currently uses German headings and a comma even though its base language is English. LC_ALL overrides the other preferences; these are actual run results.

practice.title: Save defaults, then repair the existing session
practice.action: Fill worked settings into the editor and choose Save locale settings. Run the sample report again: the existing session is unchanged. Run unset LC_ALL, then export LC_NUMERIC=C, and run the report again.
practice.observe: The running sample now has English headings, complete characters and decimal points. Saved file edits and process changes solve different parts of the handover.

concepts.title: A locale is a set of language and formatting choices
concepts.text: LANG supplies a default. LC_MESSAGES selects the sample application’s headings, LC_NUMERIC selects its decimal separator, and LC_CTYPE selects its character encoding. C uses ASCII; the supplied UTF-8 locales can represent accented and non-Latin names. locale -a lists only this activity’s supplied choices.

concepts.title: Read the effective setting, not just the default
concepts.text: A nonempty LC_ALL overrides every category. Otherwise a category’s own setting wins, then LANG, then C. Type locale to inspect the process. locale charmap shows its character encoding; locale -k decimal_point labels the actual numeric separator. Changing LANG alone cannot defeat an existing LC_ALL.

concepts.title: Process changes and saved defaults are different
concepts.text: In the terminal, export NAME=value changes this simulated session’s program environment; unset NAME removes an override. Quotes keep one value together. The native /etc/locale.conf editor saves defaults for a separate login; LC_ALL is not allowed in that systemd file. Saving does not alter a program already running.

concepts.text: Run sample report reads the selected supplied UTF-8 item;cents document. This original demonstration application formats whole cents and uses its own English/German headings; it is not a Linux utility. Open fresh login starts from saved defaults, not as a child of this terminal. Check work tests both current and fresh-login reports with different inputs.

goal: Convert and save text using the correct source encoding; diagnose and repair incomplete or changed output.
context: Builds on file and terminal foundations. All files, settings and execution are supplied by this simulator.

Use each supplied input’s stated encoding. Preserve every character and newline; valid UTF-8 with changed text or a partial conversion is insufficient.
Keep the supplied originals unchanged. Viewing conversion output alone does not save the required files.

practice.title: Compare a preview with the actual files
practice.action: Run ls /work. Run iconv -f ISO-8859-1 -t UTF-8 /work/demo-latin1.txt without -o. Inspect Actual last run, then choose Check work before saving any outputs.
practice.observe: The preview contains Thé and façade, but no required output file exists. A correct-looking terminal result is not yet saved work.

practice.action: Run the worked iconv commands with -o for demo-fixed.txt, demo-counts.txt and demo-notes.txt. Choose each saved output in Inspect document, then Check work.
practice.observe: The Latin-1 source needs conversion; ASCII remains the same bytes in UTF-8; existing UTF-8 keeps its characters. The saved copies, rather than the command spelling, are graded.

practice.title: Observe partial output and repair it
practice.action: Run iconv -f ISO-8859-1 -t ASCII -o /work/demo-fixed.txt /work/demo-latin1.txt. Inspect that output and Check work. Retry the same output path with -t UTF-8.
practice.observe: The ASCII attempt stops before é and leaves only Th. Its nonzero status matters even though a file was created. Correct conversion restores the complete saved text.

concepts.title: Characters and bytes are different
concepts.text: The same character can use different bytes. é is E9 in ISO-8859-1, but C3 A9 in UTF-8. LANG changes a program’s preferences; it does not rewrite an imported file. The supplied file labels state their source encoding so you do not have to guess.

concepts.title: Name the source and destination encodings
concepts.text: iconv -f FROM -t TO INPUT converts from one stated encoding to another. ISO-8859-1, ASCII and UTF-8 are different choices. An already UTF-8 document should not be decoded as Latin-1; that can produce valid UTF-8 containing the wrong characters.

concepts.title: Viewing is different from saving
concepts.text: Without -o, converted bytes appear in Actual last run. Add -o OUTPUT to save a separate virtual file. Supplied inputs are read-only here; real tools can replace files, so choose a different output name. Select the saved output in Inspect document to read what was actually written.

concepts.title: A failed conversion may leave a partial file
concepts.text: ASCII cannot represent é. A conversion may stop after writing the earlier characters, return a nonzero status and leave a shorter output. Read the error, correct the encoding and retry. Check work compares actual saved bytes and characters for every required file; a successful preview or a merely valid UTF-8 file is not enough.

worked.explanation: ASCII characters already have the same byte values in UTF-8, but the required output still has to be saved.

worked.explanation: Validate and copy the existing Unicode text. Treating these input bytes as Latin-1 would change its characters.
