goal: Set a regional default, then explain why its local reading can change while the UTC instant stays the same.
context: Builds on terminal and locale foundations. Supplied timestamps and all configuration are virtual; the examples and assignment have separate work.
requirements: Save Europe/Berlin as this machine’s default time zone, keeping its supplied UTC instant unchanged.
Verify both supplied instants in the current process and a separate login, including the regional offset before and after the change.
A UTC-only command display or a process override alone does not meet the saved-default requirement.

concepts.title: One instant can have several local readings
concepts.text: UTC is a shared reference for an instant. A time zone changes how that same moment is written; it does not move the underlying clock. In the worked example, 12:00 UTC is 07:00 in New York in winter and 08:00 in summer.

concepts.title: A named region includes its clock-change rules
concepts.text: Choose a regional name such as America/New_York rather than adding a fixed number of hours. Different regions need not change on the same day. This activity supplies fixed 2026 rules for UTC, Berlin, New York and Kolkata.

concepts.title: A saved default is different from one command’s view
concepts.text: timedatectl show -p Timezone --value reads the configured name; set-timezone saves a supplied region. readlink /etc/localtime shows the corresponding virtual zoneinfo link. date -u requests UTC for that command only. None of these operations changes this activity’s underlying instant.

concepts.title: Inspect a sample without setting the clock
concepts.text: Type a command in Simulated terminal, then choose Run command. date --date=@NUMBER displays one supplied Unix timestamp; it does not set the clock. The lab gives these whole-second counts from 1970-01-01 UTC—you do not need to calculate them.

concepts.title: Read the output format
concepts.text: In date '+%F %T %z %Z', %F means year-month-day, %T hours:minutes:seconds, %z the numeric UTC offset and %Z its abbreviation. + marks an output format; the quotes keep it together. date +%s prints whole Unix seconds, which stay unchanged when a zone changes.

worked.label: 1. Inspect the different example’s saved policy
worked.explanation: Expected before repair: UTC. This is a preview of the example’s initial policy, not an actual terminal result.

worked.label: 2. Read the supplied winter example
worked.explanation: Expected before repair: 2026-01-15 12:00:00 +0000 UTC. Run it to see actual output below the terminal.

worked.label: 3. Record the unchanged underlying instant
worked.explanation: This returns the example’s supplied winter instant as whole seconds. Compare it again after changing only the regional default.

worked.label: 4. Save the worked regional default
worked.explanation: This changes the example’s virtual localtime policy; it does not alter the clock or the independent assignment.

worked.label: 5. Read the winter instant again
worked.explanation: Expected repaired winter output: 2026-01-15 07:00:00 -0500 EST. This is the supplied UTC instant displayed under the saved New York policy.

worked.label: 6. Read the summer instant
worked.explanation: Expected repaired summer output: 2026-07-15 08:00:00 -0400 EDT. The region supplies a different seasonal offset without moving the underlying instant.

worked.label: 7. Compare a UTC-only view
worked.explanation: Expected: the original UTC reading for virtual now. Running date without -u still uses the newly saved regional default.

practice.title: Inspect what is saved and what is displayed

goal: Make a process follow the machine’s regional policy now and after a handover, without pinning it to today’s region.
context: Builds on the saved-default lesson. The terminal represents one report process; later policy checks are isolated samples, not changes you must apply to today’s machine.
requirements: Keep the current Europe/Berlin system default and repair the reporting process so both supplied instants follow that default.
The same process must also follow the supplied later UTC and America/New_York defaults; Check work tries those handovers separately, so do not change today’s Berlin setting for them.
Preserve the underlying UTC instant and verify the numeric offset: equal local clock readings can refer to different instants.

concepts.title: A program can choose a different time zone
concepts.text: A process is a running program. Its exported TZ setting can override the machine’s default for programs it starts. In this activity TZ is supplied by the sample report’s environment; you inspect or remove it rather than creating a user profile.

concepts.title: Compare the default with the override
concepts.text: timedatectl show -p Timezone --value reads the machine default. printenv TZ reads the report process’s exported value. date uses that value if present, so changing an already-correct machine default may not fix the report.

concepts.title: Empty and unset are different
concepts.text: export TZ= sets an empty value, which requests UTC. unset TZ removes the override, so the process follows the machine default again. After removal, printenv TZ returns exit status 1 with no text: that means the value is absent, not that the syntax is wrong.

concepts.title: Verify policy, not just one matching reading
concepts.text: A hardcoded process region can match today’s machine setting and still fail a later handover. Check work also tries the supplied later defaults with that same process environment. Keep the current requested system default while fixing the process.

concepts.title: Keep the offset with the local time
concepts.text: date '+%F %T %z %Z' prints the numeric UTC offset and zone abbreviation. Around an autumn clock change, two different instants can have the same local hour; their offsets distinguish them. The supplied UTC instants never change.

worked.label: 1. Inspect the different example’s system default
worked.explanation: Expected: Asia/Kolkata. That regional policy uses +0530 for both supplied example instants; the report’s current output still needs investigation.

worked.label: 2. Inspect the report’s own setting
worked.explanation: Expected before repair: UTC. This running process is overriding its otherwise-correct machine default.

worked.label: 3. Observe the actual masked reading
worked.explanation: Expected before repair: 2026-02-01 06:00:00 +0000 UTC. The saved Kolkata default has not been applied to this process view.

worked.label: 4. Remove the unwanted process override
worked.explanation: Remove the supplied override so this report follows its machine’s default now and after a future regional handover.

worked.label: 5. Verify the February instant
worked.explanation: Expected repaired output: 2026-02-01 11:30:00 +0530 IST. Removing the override restores the saved Kolkata policy for this report.

worked.label: 6. Verify the August instant
worked.explanation: Expected repaired output: 2026-08-01 11:30:00 +0530 IST. Check work also verifies that the same process follows the supplied later defaults.

worked.label: 7. Confirm absence rather than an empty value
worked.explanation: Expected after removal: exit status 1 and no standard output. export TZ= would instead keep an empty value and force UTC.

practice.title: Find why the report ignores its machine
practice.action: Run the worked timedatectl show, printenv TZ and February date commands separately. Compare their actual results before changing the machine’s configuration.
practice.observe: The default is Kolkata, while the supplied process override requests UTC. Saving another default alone would leave that override in effect.

practice.title: Repair the process and verify independent cases
practice.action: Run the worked unset TZ command. Query both February and August instants, then choose Check work. Run printenv TZ again and read its exit status.
practice.observe: Current, separate-login and supplied future-default cases now follow the intended policy. An absent exported value correctly produces status 1 in printenv; it does not fail the assignment.

practice.title: Diagnose empty and hardcoded overrides
practice.action: Try export TZ= and Check work; then try export TZ=Asia/Kolkata and check again. Repair with unset TZ and retry without changing the saved Kolkata default.
practice.observe: Empty TZ forces UTC. Pinning the report to Kolkata repairs today’s views but fails a later regional handover. Feedback identifies which contexts still fail.

worked.explanation: A protocol-specific key reads the virtual name database, not a running server.

worked.label: Separate example

concepts.title: An address finds a computer; a port finds a service
concepts.text: Several programs can accept traffic on one computer. A client needs the server address plus a transport, TCP or UDP, and a port number. TCP uses a connection; UDP sends separate messages. Here the server address and path are supplied, so investigate only the transport and service selection.

concepts.title: A service name is a reference, not a running program
concepts.text: A services-file line such as http 80/tcp www gives the primary (canonical) name http, port 80, transport tcp and alias www, another name for the same entry. Run getent services www/tcp to look it up. Exit 0 means a matching entry; exit 2 means no entry. cat /etc/services displays the supplied virtual file. Neither command starts a server or proves one is listening.

concepts.title: Compare the lookup with the supplied listener
concepts.text: In the worked example, browser needs the web listener on TCP 80. www and decimal 80 select that destination; ssh selects another open port, TCP 22, and is wrong for this task even if a payload arrives. time-client needs the supplied clock listener on UDP 123. A protocol-specific name can be absent even when that name exists for the other transport.

concepts.title: Check available and unavailable cases
concepts.text: Choose the transport and enter a service name, alias or decimal port in each client row. Check clients runs separate sample requests with the listener available and removed. Correct selection remains correct during the supplied outage; the expected result then is no listener, not successful delivery. Payloads here are simple sample text, not real HTTP, NTP or SSH messages.

context: Prerequisite: Linux host-networking investigations; the server address and path are supplied. No prior service-name database knowledge is assumed.

goal: Repair the saved service-name mappings

worked.label: Lookup syntax

worked.label: Separate example

concepts.title: A wrong reference can send a client to the wrong open port
concepts.text: Service names do not define the server’s listening ports. In this example http and ssh have exchanged their port numbers in the virtual file. The server still listens for web on TCP 80 and remote on TCP 22. getent services www/tcp reveals the misleading 22/tcp mapping; a delivered payload alone cannot prove it reached web.

concepts.title: Read and repair the fields
concepts.text: A line has the form name port/transport aliases, followed optionally by a # comment. For the separate worked example, change http to 80/tcp while keeping alias www; change ssh to 22/tcp. Leave ntp 123/udp time-sync unchanged. Names and aliases are case-sensitive. Both the canonical name and every existing alias must keep the required meaning.

concepts.title: Save changes before a new lookup
concepts.text: Edit /etc/services in the virtual editor and choose Save virtual file. The next getent query and client check read that saved text. An unsaved editor change has no effect on lookup. Saving does not restart a program or move the supplied server listener. Syntax errors can be saved for diagnosis, but they cannot pass a lookup or assignment check.

concepts.title: Preserve meaning rather than copying a file
concepts.text: Comments, whitespace and record order may differ. Equivalent name-to-port mappings pass; deleting unrelated names or aliases fails even if the listed client requests pass. The bounded exercise refuses ambiguous repeated per-protocol names/ports and unsupported protocols, rather than pretending to implement every Linux provider.

context: Prerequisites: the Linux host-networking unit, including IPv4 address and route investigations. IPv6 notation and the commands used here are introduced below; experienced learners may open Assignment directly.

concepts.title: Two address forms mean two separate route tables
concepts.text: IPv4 addresses have 32 bits, normally written as four decimal numbers. IPv6 addresses have 128 bits, written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits; a group can contain 0–9 and a–f. Leading zeroes in a group may be omitted, and :: can shorten one run of zero groups. 2001:db8:60::12 is an IPv6 address, not an IPv4 address with a different spelling. ip -4 and ip -6 inspect or change different tables.

concepts.title: Keep the network part and choose an unused device address
concepts.text: A /n prefix keeps the first n bits as the network part. The worked IPv4 /27 leaves five of 32 bits for devices: 2 to the fifth power is 32 addresses. Its mask is 255.255.255.224. On 10.60.5.0/27, .0 names the network and .31 is broadcast in this conventional exercise; choose an unused .1–.30 address, excluding supplied peers/gateways. IPv6 /64 keeps the first 64 bits. IPv6 has no broadcast, so do not copy the IPv4 subtract-two rule. In this exercise, the IPv6 address with every device bit zero (2001:db8:60:: in the example) is reserved for subnet-router anycast; choose another unused value and avoid supplied peers/routers.

concepts.title: A next hop belongs to an address family and a link
concepts.text: default in the IPv4 table means 0.0.0.0/0; default in the IPv6 table means ::/0. Each is used only when its family has no more-specific matching route. A link-local IPv6 next hop such as fe80::1 needs a device name: fe80::1 on ens3 and the same text on ens4 identify different neighbors. The more-specific management routes must keep ens4 even after both defaults are repaired.

concepts.title: Read evidence, repair one family and verify both
concepts.text: Start with ip -4 address show, ip -6 address show and their route show commands. This bounded workspace models one chosen primary address per family/interface, so remove the exact old address before adding a replacement. Run applies only the virtual command you typed; it cannot touch the host. The native Test address · simulator control accepts either family and derives paths from supplied facts, not actual ping/ICMP. Private and documentation addresses here describe an isolated example network, not a connection to the Internet. General IPv6 neighbor discovery, automatic addressing and multicast are outside this task.

worked.label: Read the IPv6 shorthand
worked.explanation: Full spelling: 2001:0db8:0060:0000:0000:0000:0000:0012. The single :: stands for the omitted zero groups; the /64 network part stays fixed.

worked.label: Worked repair 1
worked.explanation: Remove the example address/prefix from ens3; leave ens4 untouched.

worked.label: Worked repair 2
worked.explanation: The example /27 has usable .1–.30 addresses; .12 is unused and is not the gateway or peer.

worked.label: Worked repair 3
worked.value: ip -4 route replace default via 10.60.5.1 dev ens3 metric 100
worked.explanation: Use the IPv4 gateway on the application link; the more-specific management route remains unchanged.

worked.label: Worked repair 4
worked.explanation: Remove the example address from the wrong IPv6 /64.

worked.label: Worked repair 5
worked.explanation: Choose an unused primary address inside the supplied IPv6 /64; there is no broadcast address.

worked.label: Worked repair 6
worked.value: ip -6 route replace default via fe80::1 dev ens3 metric 100
worked.explanation: The device makes this link-local next hop unambiguous; the IPv4 default is unaffected.

goal: Restore Echo round trips and report delivery while retaining the UDP restriction
requirements: Repair the supplied R1 policy so both ICMP Echo queries complete their round trips and both TCP report conversations deliver the unchanged supplied content to the Server service on TCP port 8443.
Keep the supplied UDP datagram blocked at R1/office inbound, even though a UDP listener uses the same number.
Keep the supplied endpoints, listeners, conversations, routes and interfaces unchanged.

practice.title: Check the starter and follow the failing direction
practice.action: Use Check configuration, then open the actual TCP and ICMP Echo traces. Compare a request with its reply, including which side owns each TCP port. The supplied endpoints and conversations can be expanded above the R1 editor.
practice.observe: Expected: requests can enter the network while return policy prevents completion. Actual trace events appear only after checking; a filtered UDP datagram alone does not complete the protection requirement.

practice.title: Repair Echo first, then compare TCP
practice.action: In the separate R1 practice document, change RETURN’s ICMP rule to the worked Echo return rule. Check configuration again. Then replace RETURN’s TCP rule with the worked report return rule and check again. You may use Fill worked settings if you want the complete separate draft; it does not run the cases.
practice.observe: Expected: both Echo round trips pass after their repair, while TCP still fails until its return ports match. The unwanted UDP datagram remains filtered; the complete protection check passes once a required TCP service crosses successfully.

practice.title: Break an assumption and retry
practice.action: Temporarily change the practice RETURN rule back to deny ICMP, then Check configuration. Restore it and retry. Use Reset example only to restart this practice; open Assignment when ready to solve the independent network.
practice.observe: Expected: TCP receipt can remain correct while Echo fails. An edit clears checked feedback, and the next check explains the failing case. Practice never changes the assignment draft.

concepts.title: An application conversation and a reachability query answer different questions
concepts.text: TCP first exchanges a connection request (SYN), a response (SYN-ACK) and confirmation (ACK). This exercise then sends one fragment of the application’s ordered byte stream. UDP sends a separate message (datagram) without that handshake or a delivery guarantee. Both use source and destination ports. ICMP carries IP control and diagnostic messages: here, Echo request type 8 and reply type 0, with code 0 and no TCP/UDP service ports.

concepts.title: A request arriving does not mean its reply returned
concepts.text: A request addresses one supplied host (unicast). If it arrives, that host sends a reply. The reply swaps the IP addresses and reflects the same identifier, sequence number and bytes; those numbers match a reply to its query. TCP replies swap both addresses and ports. An Echo round trip can pass while TCP fails; a filtered Echo alone cannot establish whether another application works. Inspect each actual case rather than treating one successful test as proof of everything.

concepts.title: Read the supplied virtual router policy
concepts.text: R1’s editor contains an IOS-style policy document inside this simulator, not a Linux script or host firewall. FORWARD applies as packets enter office from Client; RETURN applies as they leave office toward Client. Read rules in numeric order: the first matching rule decides. permit allows; deny blocks; host selects one address. The lists and interface bindings are already supplied, so focus on the rules.

concepts.title: Match the correct side of a return packet
concepts.text: In a TCP rule, a port condition after the first address matches the source; after the second address it matches the destination. A service reply has the service port as its source and the client’s chosen port as its destination. range selects a span of port numbers. ICMP has no such port condition. TCP and UDP may have different listeners at the same numeric port.

concepts.title: Verify useful traffic and the restriction together
concepts.text: Check configuration runs both TCP conversations, the unwanted UDP datagram and both Echo queries. It derives every result from the current policy. The protection check also requires useful TCP traffic to cross that boundary, so an isolated drop is not a complete fix. Permit-all loses the unwanted-traffic requirement; deny-all loses useful traffic. This bounded model sends no real packets and does not implement ICMP errors, ICMPv6 or wire checksums.

worked.label: Read a returning report packet
worked.explanation: Service 9443 is the source on the return path; client 50123 is the destination. The other supplied client uses 60101.

worked.label: Worked Echo return rule
worked.explanation: In RETURN, allow the supplied server-to-client ICMP direction. Echo has no application ports; the policy matcher does not filter individual ICMP types.

worked.label: Worked report return rule
worked.value: 10 permit tcp host 10.90.4.20 eq 9443 host 10.90.3.10 range 49152 65535
worked.explanation: Match source service 9443 and both supplied high client ports. This is the separate practice network, not the assignment.

worked.label: Retain the UDP restriction
worked.explanation: In FORWARD, the unwanted UDP datagram stays blocked even though a listener uses the same number. Keep the final deny and existing interface bindings.

goal: Restore the complete application path and verify replies while preserving management.
context: Builds on Linux host networking, mixed-IP fundamentals, endpoint ownership and the protocol-evidence lesson. Use the Command field and Run command; these commands act only inside the supplied virtual network.

concepts.title: Start with one small question, then compare another destination
concepts.text: ping -c 1 asks for one Echo reply; -c sets the count. In this lesson the simulator evaluates one supplied IPv4 query immediately, with no real network or measured timing. A nearby peer can reply while a farther peer fails. Compare those observations with ip -4 address show and ip -4 route show before changing settings.

concepts.title: An address is only local under its configured prefix
concepts.text: In the worked network, ens3’s real LAN is 10.110.64.0/20. The mask 255.255.240.0 groups third-octet values into blocks of 16: 64–79 is this block. A workstation configured as 10.110.67.10/24 instead treats only 10.110.67.x as directly local. It can reach its nearby peer yet select a gateway for 10.110.78.20. Restore the supplied LAN prefix; do not assume subnet boundaries always sit in the fourth octet.

concepts.title: Read the most specific matching route before the default
concepts.text: A default covers destinations without a longer matching prefix. A host route ending /32 describes one destination and wins over /0 regardless of its metric. After correcting the default, inspect a stale application-specific route too. In this exercise, delete an interface’s gateway routes before removing its address; supported deletion needs the complete shown route fields.

concepts.title: A missing reply does not locate the fault by itself
concepts.text: The simulator models outward delivery, the peer’s response and its separate return path. A destination listed as available is not a promise that it answers Echo. The supplied silent control intentionally does not reply. Check the other working peers and the configuration outcomes; do not break a working path to make that control answer. Echo does not prove a TCP/UDP application listener is running.

worked.label: Read the worked LAN boundary
worked.explanation: Mask 255.255.240.0. In octet 3: 256 − 240 = 16. The workstation’s third octet, 67, and the far peer’s, 78, both belong to the 64–79 block.

worked.label: Correct the worked workstation prefix
worked.value:
ip -4 address del 10.110.67.10/24 dev ens3
ip -4 address add 10.110.67.10/20 dev ens3
worked.explanation: Remove the old primary address before adding the corrected prefix. Then ping -c 1 10.110.78.20 checks the farther LAN peer.

worked.label: Correct the worked default
worked.value: ip -4 route replace default via 10.110.64.1 dev ens3 metric 5
worked.explanation: The corrected /20 makes this supplied gateway on-link. A matching /32 can still override this route.

worked.label: Remove the worked detour and test again
worked.value:
ip -4 route del 10.111.8.20/32 via 198.51.100.1 dev ens4 metric 1
ping -c 1 10.111.8.20

goal: Find why an application receives a stale address, repair the client, and prove the fix survives a changing DNS answer.
context: Builds on local aliases, name-source order and DNS search. You edit two virtual file excerpts and inspect supplied IPv4 DNS samples; the resolver search settings are already provided.

concepts.title: Ask the same lookup path as the application
concepts.text: getent ahostsv4 NAME requests IPv4 addresses through the hosts name-service database. Type it in the simulated terminal and choose Run command, or press Enter. A successful result shows the address for stream, datagram and raw socket types; these are three uses of one address, not three different computers. Status 0 means a result was found; status 2 with no output means the requested name was not found. The separate simulator trace explains how that result was chosen.

concepts.title: Local aliases can hide a changing service
concepts.text: In a hosts row, the first name is the canonical name and later names are aliases for the same address. files checks the original supplied name. A successful local alias normally stops the lookup, even if DNS has a newer address. Keep deliberate rescue names local, but remove aliases that now belong to DNS instead of deleting the entire protected row.

concepts.title: A missing local name must reach the DNS search
concepts.text: The hosts: row in nsswitch.conf selects sources and what happens after each result. files dns normally continues after a local miss. files [NOTFOUND=return] dns stops too early. Only after reaching dns does the supplied search list try suffixes in order and stop on its first answer. It does not try each expanded name in the local hosts file again. A final dot makes a DNS name absolute.

concepts.title: Check the repair, not just one successful query
concepts.text: Run command investigates one selected sample using your current editor drafts. Run lookups grades all requirements across both samples. Compare the expected and actual answers and sources: a stale address can be a successful lookup but still fail the task. Do not copy one DNS address into hosts; the service address changes between samples.

concepts.title: Recognize systemd-resolved on a real Linux host
concepts.text: Some Linux systems use systemd-resolved, a local name-resolution service with a DNS stub and cache. Applications may reach it through NSS using the resolve module or through its local DNS listener. That is a different resolution path with additional rules, so a real investigation first identifies which resolver is active. This activity models only files plus dns and traditional search settings; it does not run or reconfigure systemd-resolved.

goal: Separate a server host key from a user’s public key and repair only the stale trust entry.

context: No personal SSH setup is required. Public identities and server/account facts are supplied.

concepts.title: The server and the user have different identities
concepts.text: SSH normally protects a connection and checks who is at each end. A server host key identifies the server. A client normally proves it holds the private key matching a separate user public key. This lab supplies public records and assumes the test client holds its stated identity; it does not open a connection or verify a signature.

concepts.title: Read one known_hosts line
concepts.text: The client’s known_hosts file records HOST KEY_TYPE PUBLIC_DATA, with an optional comment. The first word names the server. ssh-ed25519 is the supplied key type; the long base64 field is its public data. Copy the verified server record, not a user’s client public key. A comment is only a label.

concepts.title: Verify a changed host before replacing its record
concepts.text: An unknown host has no saved record. A changed-key result means the saved and presented public data differ. Here the administrator’s verified server record is supplied as the trusted comparison. Correct that host’s entry and preserve the separate archive entry; bypassing trust is not a repair.

concepts.title: Save, then compare two client requests
concepts.text: Typing changes the draft. Save file changes this client’s virtual trust document. Check access reads saved trust and the supplied server/account data. The administrator should pass while the different user identity remains refused at the authorized-key stage. Blocking both at host trust does not meet the task.

context: You already know that a file stores text. This lesson introduces an editor that uses different modes for movement and typing. No terminal or shell knowledge is needed.

concepts.title: Open file, buffer and mode
concepts.text: The supplied file is already open. The editor shows a working copy, called a buffer; changing it does not change the saved file yet. NORMAL means keys are editing commands. Click inside the editor to focus it. Tab moves to the next app control; it does not insert a tab.

concepts.title: Move first, then type
concepts.text: In NORMAL, h moves left, j down, k up and l right. Arrow keys also move in NORMAL. 0 means the start of the line; $ means its last character. Press i to type before the cursor or a to type after it. INSERT means letters become text. Backspace erases the preceding character, including a line break. Escape returns to NORMAL and keeps the editor focused.

concepts.title: Correct and save
concepts.text: In NORMAL, x deletes the character under the cursor. At the end of a line it moves back to the remaining last character. u undoes the most recent change; a whole INSERT session is one change. Type :w and press Enter to write the saved virtual file. Check saved files grades those saved contents and refuses unfinished drafts.

concepts.title: Read the small configuration
concepts.text: These sample records use key=value. The words on the left name settings; the text on the right is their value. Lines starting with # are comments. This exercise edits text only; it does not start a service or run the file.

context: Builds on Repair a file using vi-style modes: movement, INSERT, Escape, undo and :w. The lines are practice records, not executable jobs.

concepts.title: Find text without counting lines
concepts.text: In NORMAL type /, then a word and Enter to search forward. ? searches backward; n repeats the last search in the same direction. Search is case-sensitive, begins after the cursor, and wraps at the file boundary. This subset accepts plain letters, digits, spaces and _-=:,@%; it diagnoses regular expressions rather than pretending to support them.

concepts.title: Copy a whole line
concepts.text: In NORMAL yy copies the current complete line into the editor’s unnamed register, an internal holding place. p puts a linewise copy below the current line; P puts it above. This register is separate from the desktop clipboard. It stays available when you move or undo.

concepts.title: Remove only the retired record
concepts.text: dd deletes the complete current line and replaces the unnamed register with that line. x instead deletes one character and stores a characterwise value; p then puts characters after the cursor. Search for the record you intend to remove before using dd. Undo with u if you remove the wrong line.

concepts.title: A buffer can be wrong while its file is safe
concepts.text: The editor opens on an accidental unsaved handover draft. The saved virtual file is still the original. Inspect Actual saved file if you need to compare them. Do not save the mistake: a correct saved file with an incorrect unsaved buffer is still unfinished.

concepts.title: Save, quit and abandon have different effects
concepts.text: :w writes the current buffer to its virtual file. :q closes only when there are no unsaved edits. :q! closes and discards the unsaved buffer; it does not erase the file. :wq writes and closes. u can also recover the previous buffer; it never silently rewrites saved bytes. Enter finishes each colon command.

concepts.title: Change files deliberately
concepts.text: Choose a supplied virtual file in Virtual file, then Open selected file. The workspace refuses to switch away from unsaved edits until you save or discard them. Read-only files can be inspected and have a draft, but writing them is refused. Once a file is closed, Open selected file reopens its saved contents.

context: Builds on the shell-environment unit and modal-file editing: variables, quotes, export, NORMAL/INSERT, search and :w. This task combines setup and a real saved-file repair.

concepts.title: A value in one shell is not automatically shared
concepts.text: EDITOR names a preferred editor for applications that consult it. EDITOR=vi sets a shell value. If EDITOR was not already exported, a subsequently started child does not receive it. A value inherited at shell startup already has its export attribute, which can make the same incomplete setup seem to work on one machine.

concepts.title: Pass the requested setting to the child
concepts.text: export marks a variable for inheritance. For example, export EDITOR=vi both sets the value and marks it. In this activity PREFERRED_EDITOR and TEAM are supplied separately for every test; your setup creates or replaces EDITOR from the supplied preference. Keep TEAM unchanged. The supplied child prints the report, so your setup should not print a replacement report.

concepts.title: An editor choice is an application convention
concepts.text: Vim is a vi-style editor that uses modes. GNU nano and Emacs are other common editors, with their own controls. Applications choose which setting they honor: for example, crontab documents VISUAL or EDITOR. This exercise's handover application reads only EDITOR and supports vi or vim through the same bounded native editor. It never runs those names on your computer.

concepts.title: Configure, open, edit and verify
concepts.text: Run setup first and inspect all sample results. Once they pass, Open handover file with selected editor uses the actual child value. Change the supplied virtual file using the editing skills you already practiced. :w writes that file; Check handover verifies both the setup behavior and the saved records. Changing setup invalidates its earlier launch and check while retaining your file draft.

goal: Configure an editor preference that reaches the handover application, then update and save its handover record.
Match a guest’s presented device and running kernel with its stored driver support, then activate and verify it.
context: Prerequisites: ordinary file/terminal use, supplied module loading and RPM package investigation. A virtual machine is a computer represented by a virtualization platform. Its Linux kernel is its own core system; a driver lets that kernel work with a presented device. This exercise supplies all records and tools—no VM preparation is needed.

concepts.title: The presented device and the image can disagree
concepts.text: An image is a saved set of Linux system files, including package records and drivers. A guest can move to a platform that presents a different network adapter. The image still contains its previous support record. Use lspci -k to inspect the represented device and actual driver in use; “installed support” does not mean that device has a working driver.

concepts.title: Compare the running kernel with the supplied records
concepts.text: In the worked example uname -r reports 6.9.0-1. modinfo shows an object’s recorded vermagic release. The supplied support packages also list Requires; the kernel package lists the corresponding Provides. Compare those values before selecting a replacement. These particular records use kernel-api as their literal dependency name; real package conventions vary.

concepts.title: Files, lookup and active drivers are separate
concepts.text: Apply package change writes the supplied image files. Because these archives have no scripts, it does not silently rebuild lookup or load a driver. depmod -a rebuilds lookup from present current-release objects; modprobe NAME loads the indexed driver and its prerequisites. Many successful module commands print nothing. Verify with observations and Check configuration.

worked.label: Read the guest kernel
worked.explanation: This example reports 6.9.0-1; compare the older support record with that value.

worked.label: Choose matching supplied support
worked.explanation: Its Requires matches the supplied kernel provider. Apply package change replaces the older record but does not load a driver.

worked.label: Rebuild lookup
worked.explanation: Index the newly present objects for the current kernel.

worked.label: Activate the adapter
worked.explanation: Load this example driver and its prerequisites; then inspect lspci -k and check the complete configuration.

practice.title: Compare the presented device, kernel and support record
practice.action: Run uname -r and lspci -k separately. In Supplied archive, compare reader-support 1.1-1 with reader-support 2.1-1; read Requires and the recorded object paths.
practice.observe: The network controller has no active driver; the older support record names a different kernel release.

practice.title: Replace support, then rebuild and load
practice.action: Choose reader-support 2.1-1, select Replace / upgrade and Apply package change. Then run depmod -a and modprobe reader_net, one at a time. Insert command only fills the example input; Run executes it.
practice.observe: Package replacement creates the matching files. The driver becomes active only after a real supported loading command.

practice.title: Verify the device and the stored image
practice.action: Run lsmod and lspci -k separately, then select Check configuration. Inspect the passing current and fresh-request outcomes and confirm the storage provider remains available.
practice.observe: Both current readiness and the separate unloaded request pass; the storage provider and kernel package remain intact.

requirements: Finish with the presented network controller using its matching current-kernel driver.
Keep its object files and lookup usable for a separate request from an unloaded sample state.
Retain the supplied active storage driver and its effective prerequisite settings.
Keep the original installed kernel package version; reinstalling that same supplied archive is allowed.
Leave no unmet declared requirements among installed packages.

goal: Distinguish an installed package, an object file, a lookup entry and a driver that is already loaded.
context: Prerequisite: the preceding guest-image support lesson, plus the supplied module and package foundations. A loaded driver instance lives in the represented kernel’s running state. Its image files and package record are stored separately. This lesson intentionally starts with a working instance and an incomplete stored image.

concepts.title: Installed, present and loaded answer different questions
concepts.text: The package record says which support archive is installed. Object presence says whether its file exists. Lookup says whether the current name can be resolved. lsmod and lspci -k describe loaded instances. Removing a file need not remove an installed record or stop a loaded instance.

concepts.title: Use Reinstall for that same version’s missing files
concepts.text: The example already records sample-support 2.1-1. Choosing Install cannot repair it merely by repeating installation. Reinstall restores the exact supplied archive. The operation does not silently load a module or rebuild lookup.

concepts.title: Verify the stored image separately
concepts.text: If depmod ran while a file was missing, its entry is absent from lookup. Restore the file and rebuild lookup. A repeated modprobe can still report success from the existing loaded instance, so Check configuration also tries a separate unloaded request. That is a model observation, not a real reboot or connectivity test.

worked.label: Observe the loaded instance
worked.explanation: sample_net is already active; that does not prove its stored object exists.

worked.label: Observe device binding
worked.explanation: This associates each presented controller with its driver in use; it does not inspect all stored files.

worked.label: Read the object directly
worked.explanation: The expected missing-object diagnostic agrees with the image inspector, despite the installed record.

worked.label: Restore stored support
worked.explanation: Apply package change restores that same archive’s files without disturbing the loaded instances.

worked.label: Restore lookup
worked.explanation: The newly present object becomes available by name; Check configuration now verifies a separate unloaded request.

practice.title: Compare the running driver with its missing file
practice.action: Run lsmod and lspci -k separately. Choose sample-support 2.1-1 in Supplied archive. Expand Inspect image objects and lookup, then run modinfo /lib/modules/6.10.0-1/kernel/drivers/sample_net.ko. Select Check configuration before repairing anything.
practice.observe: Current readiness passes while the stored image’s fresh request fails. Missing file and absent lookup are separate facts.

practice.title: Restore the same version and repair lookup
practice.action: Keep sample-support 2.1-1 selected, choose Reinstall and Apply package change. Observe that the file is Present but the driver’s lookup is still Absent. Run depmod -a, then modinfo sample_net.
practice.observe: Reinstall restores the file; depmod restores lookup. The running driver remains loaded throughout.

practice.title: Verify a fresh request without stopping storage
practice.action: Run modprobe sample_net, then select Check configuration. Compare the current-driver and fresh-request outcomes. To explore afterward, remove the example support package and check again; restore it with Install and rebuild lookup if needed.
practice.observe: A full check passes only while the image still supports a separate unloaded request; deleting its support invalidates that result.

goal: Reconcile running drivers with stored image support for both the network and storage controllers.
context: Prerequisites: the preceding migration and missing-object recovery lessons. This capstone combines their faults. The running instances are still present, while the stored image is incomplete. Plan the repair from the evidence; do not treat a successful current request as proof that the next unloaded request will work.

concepts.title: Start with every required device
concepts.text: A handover can be partly correct: the network driver can be repairable while storage’s stored object is missing. Inventory both controllers, package records and lookup before changing anything. The assignment checks each required device, not only the one whose command was most recently run.

concepts.title: Respect dependency and preservation requirements
concepts.text: The guide’s kernel package provides 6.11.0-1, while its older support record requires another release. These supplied native transactions admit only a result with their declared requirements satisfied. Replace or remove the incompatible support record before other package repair. Reinstall the original kernel archive to restore missing support without changing its version.

concepts.title: Verify current and unloaded requests independently
concepts.text: Keep the active storage provider and its prerequisite settings. Package file repair does not require dismantling that provider. Rebuild lookup after restoring the image, then use Check configuration to test both devices now and from separate unloaded sample states. These checks do not reboot or prove actual disk/network traffic.

worked.label: Inventory the guide
worked.explanation: Both drivers are in use. The image inspector and initial full check expose additional stored-image faults.

worked.label: Resolve incompatible support
worked.explanation: Restore support whose declared kernel requirement matches the supplied provider.

worked.label: Restore missing storage support
worked.explanation: Restore this original archive’s object files while retaining its installed version and running storage instance.

worked.label: Verify the complete image
worked.explanation: Rebuild lookup, then Check configuration evaluates current and separate unloaded requests for both controllers.

practice.title: Inventory both running devices and the image faults
practice.action: Run uname -r, lsmod and lspci -k separately. Select Check configuration, then inspect guide-support 1.1-1 and guide-kernel 6.11.0-1. Expand Inspect image objects and lookup to locate the missing records.
practice.observe: Some current-driver checks pass, but both fresh requests and the incompatible package requirement need attention.

practice.title: Repair support and restore the protected archive
practice.action: Choose guide-support 2.1-1, Replace / upgrade and Apply package change. Then choose guide-kernel 6.11.0-1, Reinstall and Apply package change. Run depmod -a. Do not remove or force-unload the active storage provider.
practice.observe: The support record and missing object are repaired. Running drivers remain present; lookup changes only when rebuilt.

practice.title: Check the whole handover and retry a partial repair
practice.action: Run lspci -k and select Check configuration. Review both controllers’ current and fresh-request results. If a check fails, use the named package/file/lookup diagnostic to repair only that state and retry; keep guide_storage and its prerequisite settings intact.
practice.observe: All required device and preservation outcomes must pass together. A partial or subsequently broken repair is not completion.

requirements: Finish with both presented network and storage controllers using their matching current-kernel drivers.
Keep object files and lookup usable for separate unloaded requests for both controllers.
Retain the supplied active storage driver and its effective prerequisite settings.
Keep the original installed kernel package version; reinstalling that same supplied archive is allowed.
Leave no unmet declared requirements among installed packages.
